speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Consideration of the motion of Mr. James Mclsaac for an address to His Excellency, the Governor General, in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King, resumed from Monday February 21.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) who entertained us last evening with an address that, no doubt, from many points of view was very interesting-although I think it must be confessed that it was in many respects hardly relevant to the motion and the amendment before the House-covered, as I took occasion to say, when moving the adjournment of the debate last night, a very considerable extent of ground. It is not my purpose or intention to take up in detail all the different matters, more or less relevant, which he introduced into that discourse. I shall content myself with dealing with what seemed, in the mind of the hon. gentleman at all events, to be the outstanding points which he sought to make, limiting myself, if I may use the expression, to "touching the high spots". That will necessarily reduce the length of my observations, because so far as I was able to appreciate his discourse the high spots, were rather conspicuous by their absence.

The hon. gentleman, I suppose in view of what had preceded in this debate, by way of finding something that might perhaps constitute a reason why this motion should be made, and a reason that might at least call for some discussion as to why we should have an election, suggested that we should have an election because there is going to be an Imperial Conference, as he described it, in the month of June. And when he mentioned "Imperial Conference", there immediately crept into his discourse a subject that he seems as incapable of keeping out of his speeches as was the famous Mr. Dick, of Dickens' creation, incapable of keeping out of his literary productions the head of King Charles. [DOT]
He gave us a dissertation upon his conception of Canada's national position, and in that he gave us another evidence of his settled determination to thwart every endeavour that may be made to assure to Canada the national status to which she has so long aspired, and to create the impression that her achievement in the direction of that full national status amounted practically to nothing. He clings-with all the determination which the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) attributes to us in what he calls our clinging to office-to the colonial garments with which he sees Canada still robed.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. I appreciate his modesty which seeks so promptly to repudiate the honours unconsciously attached to him. However that may be from the point of view of the hon. gentleman, perhaps* I should apologize for the error; it is always proper to apologize in such a case.
Mr.'LEMIEUX: And sin no more.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman, in his frantic endeavour to establish that Canada is, after all, nothing but a mere colony, carries us back to 1911. Incidentally, I may suggest that in seeking to establish that position he is seeking to establish that a large part of the life-work of his late distinguished leader, for whom he professes so great admiration, went absolutely for naught. But the hon. gentleman is still living in 1911. May I say to him that since 1911 a great deal of water has passed under the bridges? And may I add that a great deal of blood has been spilled on the battlefields of a ravaged and devastated Europe? And may I further add-but it is not needful to remind the hon. gentleman of that-that much of that blood was the blood of Canada's youthful sons Who, if nothing else had proved it, proved to the world that Canada had bought, at a price that is beyond all prices, the right to recognition of that nationhood to which she had grown? The hon. gentleman, going back to 1911, cites a declaration of the then Prime Minister of Great Britain, Right Hon. Mr. Asquith, that it was impossible that the dominion nations of this Empire should ever have any share in the control of the Empire's foreign affairs. Having cited this, the hon. gentleman says:	The case is
ended; that is conclusive; there is nothing more to be said. I would ask the hon. gentleman: Since when have the people of Canada decided that their destinies are to be settled by the ipse dixit of any British Prime Minister, no matter how distinguished he may be? Time out of mind and times without number there has been hurled across the floor from the other side- we have heard it from the hon. gentleman himself-the imputation that upon this side of the House there was some desire to be governed from Downing Street. What more absolute evidence of the Readiness to be governed from Downing Street can be found than the abject submission of the hon. gentleman and his friends to a declaration, which he attributes to one Prime Minister, as settling forever the national status of Canada? In that day what that Prime Minister said was unsound and untrue. He slammed the door in the face of Sir Joseph Ward, who had made the suggestion-which, I am sure, found a response in the hearts of the people of all these dominions-that the time had come when as sister nations we were entitled to have our say as to what the Empire of which we are an essential part should do in connection with her foreign affairs as well as in connection with

other affairs of general interest. We have to admit that the then representative of this Dominion stood silently by, and so far as silence could give acquiescence he gave his acquiescence. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) is not satisfied with that silent acquiescence; he comes to ,us now, ten years afterwards, to proclaim that the question was then and there settled once for all. May I remind him that there were people in Canada at that time who were not prepared to give that silent acquiescence? May I remind him that within one year after that incident other representatives of Canada were in England speaking the real voice of Canada? May I remind him that among those gentleman was the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden)? May I recall to his mind also the fact that that right hon. gentleman went from gathering to gathering in England proclaiming in terms that permitted of no misunderstanding that Canada did not accept the dictum that she . never could and never would have a voice in the control and direction of those important affairs touching so closely her vital interests? Has he forgotten-or, perchance, did he never know-that that same Mr. Asquith (who in the presence of the acquiescing representatives of Canada had slammed the door in Sir Joseph Ward's face) after these pronouncements of the right hon. member for King's and after the response that he saw they evoked in the British hearers of that right hon. gentleman, reopened that door? What Mr. Asquith said in 1911 he abandoned in 1912, the hon. member clings to it still. Let me read to him what the hon. Mr. Asquith said in 1912 after he had heard the real voice of Canada as spoken by the right hon. member for King's. It may be found in the British Hansard for the 22nd of July, 1912. In what he acknowledged there Mr. Asquiths did not stand alone; there was a veritable chorus of leaders and leading statesmen on both sides of the British House declaring their recognition of the soundness of the doctrine that the right hon. gentleman was laying down, and Mr. Asquith's statement came as the crowning of what they had all said. And what did Mr. Asquith say? I quote from the British Hansard:
I will add, although I will not make any detailed statement upon that point at this moment-that side by side with this growing participation in the active burdens of the Empire, on the part of our Dominions there rests with us undoubtedly the duty of making such response as we can to their obviously reasonable appeal that they should be entitled to 
be heard in the determination of the policy and in the direction of Imperial affairs. I do not say it would be wrong to state-of course Mr. Borden and his colleagues would be the first to disclaim any desire for any such declaration, but I do not say in what shape or by what machinery that great purpose is to be obtained. Arrangements like that cannct be made in a day. They must be the result of mature deliberation and thought; they will probably have to develop from time to time-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will show the hon.
gentleman how they have developed from time to time. There was a period of time filled with great events between 1912 and 1921. Mr. Asquith continues:
- but without committing ourselves in any degree to particular forms in the matter, we share with our great Dominions the feeling which has become more and more conscious and articulate as years have gone on throughout the Empire, that we have a common heritage and interests, and that in the enjoyment of that heritage, and in the discharge of the duties which those interests involve, we ought more and more to be conscious partners with one another.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Hear, hear. Fine
words.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
As the then Prime
Minister of Great Britain foresaw, time has done its developing work. The hon. gentleman-I should say the hon. gentlemen, for the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) insists upon being included-seem to be singularly blind to what is going on around them. They have not seen this developing work of time in which their late leader had so implicit a faith. They do not seem to have the aspirations that he had. They want to see their Canada always, shall I say, in her swaddling clothes?- Perhaps that would be carrying things too far; but however she may grow, whatever years she may attain, whatever achievements may be to her credit, however perfectly she may have fitted herself for her role amongst her sister nations, they want to see her with her fingers grasping close her mother's apron strings and clamouring to be kept in the nursery. High ambition, lofty ideal, for Canadians to hold! Surely the hon. gentlemen, who after all, I know have good Canadian hearts, will some day wake up, will some day escape from their Egyptian darkness which seems to surround them and precludes their seeing their country's growth. I spoke of their being in Egyptian darkness. Is this blindness of theirs perhaps not more attributable to the very dazzling nature of the light that shines upon this country and shows her forth to the world's nations as a nation

standing on a footing of equality amongst the nations of the British Commonwealth? Is is not rather that, on account of their having accustomed themselves to live in the darkness of that colonial condition, the light appears to be too much for their unaccustomed eyes, and just because the evidence is too conclusive, because the light shines too brilliantly, they seem incapable of seeing?
I have said that through those years there have been developments. Certainly a great change operated from the day of the British Prime Minister's declaration cited by the hon. gentlemen in which he pooh-poohed the possibility of the Dominions standing recognized as sister nations, to the day when another Prime Minister of Great Britain, introducing the representatives of those sister nations into the society of nations, first at the Paris conference and in the League that was subsequently constituted, said, mincing no words:	" Why, Sir, these are practically
independent nations." There is a long gap between those two declarations, and evidently the moving hand of time of which Mr. Asquith spoke in 1912 had not stopped but had continued to move during that period. What is the evidence that has satisfied the world of Canada's national status and that has left unconvinced no one but a few-I sincerely believe they are becoming fewer-people in Canada who persist in turning their eyes away from, the light? It is not my habit, nor my practice, to try to search out men's motives; I am satisfied to judge their actions, and as I have said, I believe that these hon. gentlemen have good Canadian hearts.. I can only wish them a better intellectual eyesight.
What is the position to-day? Every statesman of the United Kingdom recognizes that this Empire is made up of different, distinct, self-governing nations, and that it takes all of them to make the great commonwealth which is called the Empire; that there belongs to no one of those nations the right of domination over the other; that there belongs not even to a majority of those nations the right to dominate over any one or more of them. We have found a better method for binding together those nations of the great British Commonwealth, because, bear in mind that I have made no suggestion that Canada or any one of the other Dominions is a nation outside of the British Empire. I have heard the hon. gentleman many and many a time in eloquent periods protest his devotion to the maintenance of that great commonwealth,
and so far as those expressions go, I have no desire to differ with him. There is in what I am saying no suggestion of any separation from the great Empire which really would be dislocated if one of these members should abandon it, and I am not talking of that; but I am trying to bring to the mind of the hon. gentleman just what that Empire is, and it is that partnership to which the Hon. Mr. Asquith aspired in the words that I have quoted. Surely we stand to-day, by common acknowledgment of the statesmen not only of the other Dominions, but of the United Kingdom itself, nations each equal in status with every other.
I do not think I need labour that further. Why did His Majesty, when he was called upon to sign the peace treaty and wanted to bind his entire Empire, sign that Treaty distinctly on behalf of Canada, distinctly on behalf of Australia, distinctly on behalf of South Africa, distinctly on behalf of New Zealand? Why did he consider that he should not impose that signature until he had the advice of his ministers of those respective countries? Simply because what was needed was the Empire's signature, and you would not have the Empire's signature when you had the signature of but one of the nations if you had not the signatures of all the nations that went to make up that Empire. Can there be any more outstanding act that His Majesty is ever called upon to do on behalf of this Empire than the signing of a treaty of that import? Why, too, when the nations proceeded to form their Assembly of Nations, did they welcome Canada as one amongst them? Why, when they convened their Assembly of the League of Nations, did they summon Canada to be present? Why did they receive her delegates on a footing of equality with the delegates of the greatest States of this world? Why did they, whatever may have been the value of what those delegates had to say, listen with respect to the voice of Canada? The answer is obvious. Nothing of that kind could have happened if they at all events had not differed from my hon. friend as to Canada's status. And now the hon. gentleman finds a reason why we are not a nation. It is because we are not performing all the actions of nations. He says-just listen, because it is so conclusive and so convincing! Why, he says, you have not got any consular offices. A new addition to the essentials of national existence! Because Canada has not felt the need of consular offices, because, having this big

sister nation, which, by reason of its manifold interests, requires such offices all over the world and is willing to give Canada the service of those offices whenever she may have an interest calling for representation in those countries-because under those circumstances Canada does not seek to provide herself with consular offices, then, forsooth, Canada has gone back to her colonial status! Having given us this conclusive reason, what is the next thing the hon. gentleman proceeds to do? He directs an attack upon this Government for having sought to provide for diplomatic representation at Washington. Very consistent! We are not a nation because we have not got consular offices; the one thing he is able to point out as lacking to our national status is that we should have consular offices; but so determined is he that we should not complete the national status that he makes an onslaught upon us for having had the ambition to provide for a diplomatic representative at Washington, the country where we have the greatest occasion for representation, the country with whom our relationships are such that we may be said, without exaggeration, to be in constant communication with regard to matters of a kind that, where we have no diplomatic representative, have to be communicated through the office in Great Britain and communicated back through that office, and through the British Ambassador to us. The hon. gentleman waxes indignant because we sought to remedy that state of affairs. Is it that he is afraid that he may be deprived of the last shred of argument that he could invoke to deny the status of his own country, to humiliate her and keep her back among the growing children who have not yet reached the status of manhood or womanhood and are not yet qualified to take their place among their adult companions in the great body of the world's nations?
Then, my hon. friend and the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) raised the ghost that we thought had long since been laid, the ghost with which they seek to terrorize the people of Canada, the ghost of some central organization that must necessarily be brought into existence and have conferred upon it a power to dominate Canada if Canada ventures to assert her national status. Outside of the imagination of these hon. gentlemen, where can we find evidence of any such danger as that? Who is preaching to-day the creation of a central organization to dominate this Dominion?

Lord
Burnham and Lord Cave.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If Lord Burnham and
Lord Cave are preaching such a doctrine, let me again point out that we on this side of the House are not like my hon. friend. We do not say:	Lord Burnham and Lord
Cave have said so; therefore, Canada, bow down.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We do not say that
either.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
We have our say. Let me just read to the hon. gentleman what somebody who has more to say about the matter than Lord Burnham or Lord Cave, so far as Canada is concerned, had to say the other day in our good city of Montreal. Speaking on this question of Imperial relations, he said:
Let us keep on the way we are going and let brotherly love continue. I have never been a believer In abrupt constitutional change. The elevation of our status as a British nation has through all the years been a matter of growth rather than of change, and so it will always be.
There are those who are continually seeing trouble In our Imperial relations, and who pretend to be In terror lest we lose our autonomy. There is no more danger of the loss of our autonomy than there is of the loss of our atmosphere. Don't let us be frightened by ghosts, especially homemade ghosts, born and re-born, exhibited and re-exhibited wholly for political purposes. One political leader of the present time-he does not live in Montreal- puts a declamation into every speech against what he calls Imperial Centralization. I don't konw anyone with the slightest Influence either here or anywhere else who wants Imperial Centralization.
He was apparently not as intimate with the noble lords as my two distinguished friends. He went on:
It is a long, long time since, any such system was even seriously talked of, and no one has done more to make anything like centralized control forever impossible and to point a more excellent way to the British' family of nations than has the man who led this country through the war, whose principle of full autonomy I adhered to then and sanction now. Perhaps the necessity of an issue is father to the thought, but there are some whose fear of centralization is the greater the farther we get from it.
Those are the words of the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country, speaking the unanimous opinion of the men who sit behind him. Will the hon. gentlemen now stop being afraid of ghosts?
They tell us they do not want Imperial centralization. Here is the declaration from the authorized voice which speaks for this side of the House. Why are gentlemen

so afraid? But perhaps before proceeding further I might remark that when one insists on remaining in the nursery one is likely to lack confidence in what oneself may do by way of protection from dangers real or apprehended. But those of us who have been proud to step out into the open field of Canada's nationhood trust to ourselves for our own protection from any threatened interference with our autonomy, if there be any such threat. And let me add that I am not aware of the statements of Lord Cave or Lord Burnham, but I have heard statesmen occupying,-with all respect to those particular gentlemen-much more prominent and much more influential positions in the Government of the British Empire, and I have heard them, not once but time and time again-and you may find their declarations in the newspapers - repudiating the idea of any such ambition. Let hon. gentlemen not be afraid; let them gather their courage together.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We do not lack that.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Then what is it that you lack?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The facts.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nothing else.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The facts? We have not a Consular office at Washington; we did try to have a minister there.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You won't have it; you cannot get it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Let us suppose, for the sake of argument, that we cannot get it. (Let me say in parenthesis that that last statement I know to be unfounded; but let us suppose it to be true). The hon. gentleman will have no nationhood because we have not that thing which he denounces as something disastrous for Canada to have. The logic, of course, is absolutely conclusive.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Don't twist.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, if the hon. gentleman is not afraid, then we may take it that the ghost has disappeared and the central organization has no terrors for him; and there is nothing left now but the fact that we might have a representative at Washington.' I am not sure whether he is afraid of our having one, or of the possibility that we might not; there is some doubt on that score.
Now, to pass from this matter, which I must apologize for having given so much
time to; my excuse is that I have regard for the hon. gentleman and would be glad to see him come out from the ways of darkness and walk with us in the paths of light;
I feel he could do a valuable service to this young nation if he only would have the faith to believe in it. The measure of Canada's nationhood is just the measure of the determination of her children to see that she has that nationhood; and if we fail in that respect it will be because the adversaries of Canada's nationhood, who are to be found only in Canada, will have succeeded, will have triumphed, will have overturned the facts by their misinterpretation of them. Canada's nationhood has no enemies outside of Canada; it is not questioned abroad; we have to come to Canada to find the thing put in question. Why, if I wanted to refer to past things, I might just mention that when in the United States Congress men were looking round for arguments against Canada's right to stand among the nations, and to have her vote cast in the assembly of those nations, having sought the world over, one of them at all events was able to find but one argument, and it was in the speech of an non. member of this House. If hon. gentlemen are proud of that role I do not envy them their conception of what is a proper subject of pride.
And now, to come to this proposition upon which the hon. gentleman hung his observations about Canada's nationhood and of which he profited as an opportunity to add his further little effort to defeat Canada's nationhood, that is, the proposition that because there is to be what he terms an Imperial Conference in June of this year therefore we ought to have a general election. I appreciate the value of the argument in so far as it is evidence that the hon. gentleman recognizes that what had been, until he made his speech, put forward as an argument, was in fact so utterly insufficient that he must go out looking for an additional reason. But it will not take a great deal of time to show that this second argument that has been brought up as a reinforcement of the failing argument advanced in support of this motion is weaker even than the beaten reason to whose reinforcement it has been called. The hon. gentleman says that because there is going to be what he describes as an Imperial Conference we must have a general election. There have been Imperial Conferences in the past; they were attended not only by the leader of our most recent Government, the right hon. member for King's, (Sir Robert Bor-



den), but during a series of years in different sessions they were attended by the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the former leader of my hon. friends opposite, and a great Canadian whose memory we all of us respect.. Did he go to the country every time he was going to attend an Imperial Conference? I do not think hon. gentlemen would be able to point to one instance in which he did. The last occasion I remember was during the sesion of 1911 when the House adjourned in order that the then Prime Minister might attend an Imperial Conference. Was any voice raised then to suggest that there was need of going to the country before the right hon. gentleman proceeded to the Imperial Conference? It is true-and I shall have something to say on this later on-that at that very time members of this House were arguing that there was reason to go to the country. But they stopped that very argument and suspended discussion of the matter in order to allow the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier to go and attend the Imperial Conference. And that was not the only Imperial Conference which the right hon. gentleman attended. If I remember rightly, he attended three; at all events he attended more than one, and he never went to the country before going to any Conference. The reason was obvious. In that, as in many other things, Sir Wilfrid Laurier was right and the Parliament of that day was absolutely right. Why should his going to an Imperial Conference involve his having a general election first? In the first place, let me say to the hon. gentleman that what is going to take place in June is not an Imperial Conference, although I am quite willing, for the purpose of this argument, that he should regard it as such. As a matter of fact, it will be a meeting of Prime Ministers to talk over and discuss matters. It is not, nor would an Imperial Conference be, a body whose decisions would bind any country represented at it.
Everybody who knows what the Imperial Conference is-and this, as I have said, is not even an Imperial Conference-knows that no country was ever bound by anything that transpired at it; that if the parties attending that conference did, as between themselves, come to a mutual agreement that a certain course would be desirable, all that could follow from it could be that the representative of each country would go back home and report-submit his report first to the government of his country, and that government, if it approved, would submit to

the national Parliament the suggested plans or projects that may have been considered and may have been agreed to at such conference. Why, we have an outstanding instance of that in the conference of 1912 where the Prime Minister of that day came back from the conference and laid before this House a project, and that project failed entirely of effect because the other Chamber of this Parliament declined to approve of it. Why then the need of going to the country before the Prime Minister can talk over with these other Prime Ministers things that may be proposed, not things that shall be done? 1 think the hon. gentleman himself will appreciate that if out of that conference there should grow anything that would call for a decision by the people of this country, the only proper time to go to the people upon questions of that sort would be when the Prime Minister had taken the responsibility of asking the Canadian Parliament to take some action with regard to it. I am not now going to discuss whether it would or would not, under those circumstances be necessary or desirable to go to the country. That would depend almost entirely-very largely at all events -upon what the nature of the proposition would be; , but to suggest that, contrary to all precedent, this House should now declare that the Prime Minister cannot go to England to talk over and discuss with the other prime ministers of the different nations of this Empire what might be in their mutual interest and what would be a desirable course for each of them to adopt, without first dissolving this House and going to, the country, is, I think, carrying the search for reasons to bolster up an unsustainable proposition to the extreme limit to which such a search can be carried. It seems to me it would not be unfair to speak of my hon. friend's position, in so far as he grasps at that contention, as the desperate grasping at a straw by the drowning man who finds that the plank to which he had entrusted himself has failed.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend will, I am sure, allow 'me to ask a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am sure that my hon. friend does not want to give a different interpretation from what I said about the next conference. I said that if the Prime Minister of Canada was going to a conference, where he is to discuss-according

to despatches which have been
4 p.m. published of late-the share that Canada must take in the naval defence of the Empire, surely that was such an important question that he should get a mandate from the people. That is what I suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. and learned friend when he does not rely upon his imagination for establishing the facts upon which he bases his conclusions falls back upon that substantial basis, "what the newspapers say about current events." As I have already stated, whatever the newspapers may say, this meeting of Prime Ministers is not going to decide anything which will hind any country. Whether they will talk about Imperial defence I am not in a position to say; but whatever may be talked about there, let the hon. gentleman possess his soul in calm-nothing will be done there that will bind Canada. From the very nature of things nothing can be done there that will bind Canada; the whole thing is purely consultative.
During the hon. gentleman's references to our providing for a minister at Washington-I do not know whether he fears we shall or shall not take that course-he went on to make some allusion to the question of water being taken from the Great Lakes for the Chicago ship canal.

a part of that humanity; let him not suggest we should abstain from doing our reasonable part to keep Canada in a position in which she may not suffer the reproach that she alone among the nations did not interest herself in that which makes for the common good of the world; let him not be afraid that because we are prepared to do our duty in that regard we are therefore going to expose the interests of this our own nation of which we are so proud.
Now, let me come to what the hon. gentleman attempted to say in support of the general proposition that this amendment was called for because the continued existence of this Parliament and of this Government was a violation of every constitutional principle. It is a very long time since I have had the pleasure-we will call it pleasure-of listening to so much variegated and strong language and so many rash assertions, made and repeated as though the makers and repeaters of them had an absolute conviction of the efficacy of the rule lately laid down by a distinguished American politician-that the one way to get a statement accepted is to make no effort to prove it, but to just throw it out and keep repeating it and getting it repeated, until finally you say: well, of course, nobody argues anything against that; it is obvious.
Our distinguished friends on the other side, starting with their leader, have told us that the war being over the remaining in office of this Government is a breach of the British constitution, and that if we do not hurry up and go to the people to-morrow that breach would hardly be reparable. They advanced reasons in support of this, citing the fact that one gentleman in Great Britain went to the country because the by-elections had been going against him; and that another gentleman who argued against the proposition at that time, had argued in favour of it when he happened to be in Opposition at another time. And, faithful to the colonial aspirations which distinguish my hon. friends on the other side, they threw at us those isolated facts as conclusive evidence that that was the spirit of the British constitution; some of them even waxed eloquent about a government " of the people, by the people, and for the people "; and, of course, as we all know, they were quoting Abraham Lincoln; and then they concluded that this House ought to dissolve to-morrow.
I wonder if the {ion. gentlemen have forgotten that the very essence of the British

constitution is parliamentary government. In the. sense which the hon. gentlemen are clamouring for, the British constitution does not provide for government by the people; it provides for government by the people's representatives, and it determines, according to the laws of the different countries, for what period of time the mandate shall be conferred upon the members of Parliament. Because, mind you, we have heard a great deal of talk about the mandate of this Government and the mandate of that Government coming directly from the people. That is an expression used at different times, but people who understand know that it is purely figurative. The mandate that the elector gives is a mandate to the member of Parliament. And my hon. [DOT] friend the leader of the Opposition seemed to think it necessary to carry us back to very ancient times for the purpose of telling us that there existed a legal remedy known as quo warranto-a remedy that exists to-day just as it has always existed -and he went on to say that by that great writ a man holding office was called upon to say by what warrant he held his office. My hon. friend then suggested that if a writ of quo warranto went to this Government it would be powerless to make a conclusive answer.
Why, if any such writ came demanding, just as the hon. gentleman with eloquent reiteration demands, by what right we are sitting here, we at once tell him: By the authority of those two bodies-if I may apply the expression to both of them-by whose authority alone any Government can hold power; we sit here by right of the fact that the Prime Minister of this country to-day, being called upon by the representative of the Sovereign to form a Government, that is to say, enjoying the confidence of the Sovereign, found that selection ratified by an expression of confidence of the majority of the Parliament of this country. There is no other warrant by which any man can hold the office of Prime Minister, there is no other warrant by which any man can be justified in occupying a position as a member of the Cabinet in any Government. All this elaboration and discussion about a mandate to the Government led by the right hon. member for Kings, (Sir Robert Borden), as distinguished from a mandate to the Government led by the right hon. gentleman who now leads it, is all built upon theories elaborated in the imaginations of the hon. gentlemen vcho set them forth.

I shall* not go into any examination of authorities on a question of that kind. Anybody, I venture to say, who knows anything about-I do not say the letter, but the spirit of the British constitution, ;"the spirit that giveth life", as my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition knows-is aware that the great distinctive feature of the British constitution which differentiates it from all those constitutions which have not directly and without distinction followed it, is the fact that its centre is the principle of parliamentary government, and that under it the great power is Ihe Parliament of the country.	[DOT]
Now, there is no doubt that the parliament of the country takes its authority from the people, but it takes the authority that the people give it, and when the people- vote for a member of parliament they vote for a man whom they are willing to charge with the function of governing during the period for which the lajsv and the constitution provide; whom they are willing to trust in regard to what may arise during that period and charge with the responsibility of dealing with it. They give him a mandate-a mandate that has to run during a fixed period, unless in the interval a Government having the confidence of the majority of parliament comes to the conclusion that by. reason of some great and new question that has arisen, or possibly, by reason of some crisis that the country is facing, it is desirable and necessary that there shall be a dissolution. But a Government that is to pronounce upon that is a Government that has the confidence of a majority of this Parliament. So long, therefore, as a majority of this Parliament stands in agreement to give its confidence to a Government the leader of which the Crown has reposed its confidence in by calling upon him to form a ministry, you have the government contemplated by the British constitution. And there are reasons for that which have no connection with a desire to cling to power and all the other sordid motives which the hon. gentleman attributed to us the other evening and poured out in the series of more or less meaningless invectives with which he closed his speech. One of the great benefits, one of the great advantages, of the British constitution, is the stability that it gives to the country. The British constitution never contemplated that the electors were going to select representatives so unfit to cope with the problems that might arise that as each particular question came up they would have to run back to the people to find out what the people wanted. The people elected men in whom they had confidence and charged them with the responsibility of dealing with the situations that might present themselves. We would afford a sorry spectacle if we should accept and act upon the doctrine of unconstitutionality which has been preached, with the result that we should have a series of powerless, spineless, irresponsible parliaments-parliaments composed of men who, though seeing before them clearly the course which their duty called upon them to follow, would not have had the courage to form their own decision and courageously follow that course, but would say " Oh, no, I had not thought of that at the last election and I did not talk about it; let me run back to the people and find out whether or not, perchance, there is at this moment some wave of public feeling that may run counter to that: to me the course is clear as to what is best for the country, but I do not care for that. I am the man who was charged with the duty of doing what I conscientiously believed to be best for the country, but that is nothing to me; perhaps there is some current of public opinion running counter; it may turn and run in the other direction to-morrow; let me hurry and get there before the current changes." That is not the British conception of government; that is not the British conception of parliament.
The hon. leader of the Opposition went over a whole list of countries that had had elections since the conclusion of the war and wanted to know whether the people of Canada were so inferior to the people of those countries that they should not be gratified with having an election. Well, in the first place, in the case of most of these countries the election was held because the parliamentary term had expired. In the case of the United States, the election was held because the constitution said that they should have an election at that particular time. Let me, in parenthesis, referring to this country where there is government " of the people, by the people and for the people." point to the fact that the people in November declared their absolute want of confidence in the existing government of the United States and that that government is carrying on still. That is according to their constitution; ours is a vast improvement on that, no doubt. I mention it only as showing how figurative all these words are.

I had said that I would not cite authorities. Let me make one exception. I shall not delve into the past; anyone who will study the works of the men who were the real authors of this Constitution may see for themselves. In that connection I would ask my hon. friend, who shares with me, If I may judge from the citations he so frequently makes from his writings and speeches, a high admiration for that eminent statesman who had much to do with the building up of the British Constitution, Edmund Burke - I would ask him to read his work and see what the constitutional system of government is under the British Constitution. Last session someone did say that Burke had gone out of fashion; that his ideas were, as John P. Robinson said, "exploded idees." I shall not go back to that, but I will read the statements of one gentleman, a statesman of our own country, who said, referring to this very question:
I take issue with my hon. friend from North Toronto and my hon. friend from Brandon when they tell us that the Parliament of Canada is debarred from dealing with any question which has not been discussed at the previous general election.
Just note the contention that is made here.
That is not in accord with the constitutional history of Great Britain or of Canada either, as I have read it. Let me ask my hon. friends what mandate had the Government of Lord Elgin in 1853, when it went to tVashington *to obtain, Reciprocity!? Hadi that question ever been put before the people? Had it been an issue the last time the people's representatives had gone before them? Not at all. Let me ask, further, what mandate had the Government in 1864 to put through Parliament the resolution which proposed Confederation a Had the question of Confederation ever been put before the people of United Canada? No, not a word about it had ever been heard,. The only question then raised was that of representation by population.
Just as we are told now that the only question in the last election was the carrying on of the war.
Yet the Government of Sir John Macdonald and the Hon. George Brown-because the two were united on that occasion-brought in a resolution which was nothing more nor le3s than a complete transformation of our then condition. When Canada assented in 1871 :o the Fishery stipulation in the Washington Treaty of that year, had that question ever been put before the people? No, it was unknown to them. It never had been debated before.
I am sorry that the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is not here; it might do him good to hear this.
In the face, therefore, of these precedents, It is childish for any man to challenge the
IMr. Doherty.]
right of this Government to follow the course it is doing.
If my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition were here he would sit back scandalized-scandalized as he is at this Government to-day. He would sit back, no doubt, and say to us: What office-holders; what men among those who love the loaves and the fishes, who make broad their phylacteries, who enlarge the borders of their garments, who love the uppermost rooms at feasts and the chief seats in the synagogues, and greetings in the marketplace, - who make clean the outside of the cup and platter and within are full of extortions and excess; - what man of this description is it that uttered the words I have just been listening to?-Tell me that I may pour out upon his devoted head the vials of my indignation, that I may search the Scriptures to find, if possible, even additional expression^ of Scriptural vituperation with which I may forever confound the name and memory of that unworthy man, that officeholder, that clinger-on to office, that lover of the loaves and fishes and all the rest of it. And, of course, I would give him a little time so that he might, in some degree regain his calm, his selfcontrol, and be able to restrain himself, and then I would tell him that the man who pronounced those words, the man who followed that doctrine consistently throughout his life, was that great Canadian statesman, the right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. whose successor the leader of the Opposition of to-day is; the man of whom I fancy the proudest thing that the present Opposition leader has to say for himself is that he was this man's devoted follower through many years; the man with regard to whom we are all prepared to say that, whatever may have been our differences with him, we respected and admired him and we especially recognized in him a distinguished authority upon constitutional questions of this kind.
I do not think I need go further to make the justification from the constitutional point of view of the position of the present Prime Minister and of this Government in refusing to be stampeded into a general election. We have a duty to do. The public of this country gave us a mandate and imposed a duty upon us, and that mandate was and that duty was to protect the interests of Canada to the best of our judgment and our capacity, until the time should come when our mandate expired under the law or when in our honest con-

viction the interests of the country called for a change, not merely in the Government, but in the Parliament of Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite have cast insult and slur upon this Government. Do they realise that they are casting insult and .slur upon every member of this Parliament? This Government is not here of its own volition; it is here because it possesses the confidence of the majority of this Parliament, and because the majority of this Parliament is convinced that the moment has not come when they would be justified in surrendering the mandate that the people gave them, when they would be justified in departing from the performance of the duty that the people, when they gave their representatives the mandate, imposed upon them.
"But," we are told, "there have been byelections, and the by-elections are going against you and they show that the public has no confidence in you." And we were referred to a list of by-elections as establishing conclusively a complete overturn in public opinion in this country. Just let us look at those by-elections for a moment. We were told that there were seventeen by-elections, in which five Liberals, and five supporters of this or the preceding Government, were re-elected. As regards those constituencies, surely we have conclusive evidence that there is absolutely no change of opinion in those constituencies from the opinion that prevailed in 1917. As regards them we are asked to say that we have lost the confidence of the public because the people who always voted against this Government are voting against it still. As regards those constituencies, the position is absolutely identical with what it was when this House was elected. What is left? With regard to constituencies in which there has been a change, let me in the first place point out that there has been no change in the direction of the party led by the leader of the Opposition, save in one case where he succeeded in getting a minority, a small minority comparatively, of the total vote of the constituency, placed in such a favourable position that it was able to say who should be the member. As regards the other constituencies they all went to gentlemen desirious of securing special representation for a special class in this Parliament. We have yet to have any evidence that the electors who elected them elected them because they wanted a dissolution of this Parliament. All that the election of those gentlemen established is that the electors of those constituencies thought it
was desirable that there should be in this House greater representation of the particular class to which they belonged. I have not heard it said that in any of those elections-Certainly it has not been said that in all those elections, the dissolution of this House was made an issue.
So, what is the proposition? Because there are six constituencies in this country which have pronounced their adherence to a party that was not in existence in 1917, you have to asume that there is so violent and widespread a change in the opinions of the electorate of this country that this House, having barely completed its third year, should immediately dissolve. Can any proposition be more utterly without of foundation?
Then, there is the one constituency to which I have referred, which had not supported the Opposition party in 1917, a constituency which has returned, by a minority vote, an adherent of the Liberal party.
I would just like to call attention to that election, in the first place from the point of view of its bearing upon this vote which we are about to take, and in the second place from the point of view of the light it throws upon the sincerity of those who are here professing to want an election. In the first place, what is the lesson of that election? The one clear lesson that results from that election is that the overwhelming majority of the people of Peterborough, whatever else they do or do not want, do not want an election. Let me explain why. Who precipitated that election and upon what issue? There was in this House a man to whom we must pay the tribute that he sincerely wanted an election, and he gave his proof,-he took his political life in his hands. He went out to the people of Peterborough and he asked them for an endorsement of the proposition that we ought to have an election now. How many votes did he get and how many people voted against that man who had made the issue, thus making it clear that they did not want an election? There were altogether something like 12,800 votes cast, and how many of them said they wanted an election? The figures show that: 2,595 electors in Peterborough wanted an election; 4,093 said: We do not want an election, we are out to fight the man who raised the standard of a new election, we want him defeated, what we want is a Liberal member in this existing House; 2,811 said we do not want an election, we want a member in this existing House to support the present Government; 2,319 said: We do

not want an election, get out and beat that man Burnham, we want a Farmer member in this existing house; 1,103 said the same thing, we do not want an election; we will not follow the standard of the man who made this election necessary; we want a Labour member in this House. The result was that you had 8,828 voters in Peterborough who upon the issue: Election or no election, said: We do not want an election; there is something else we want more. You had only 2,595 who said they wanted an election.

They have been
voiceless on the subject of whether they wanted an election. All I know is that they wanted elected, at the risk of defeating the man who raised the standard of an election or no election, a Liberal member to sit in this House.

speechtext: He will tell us when he comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
