speechtext:
Probably he will. When he gets here, he will probably be anxious to forget the platform upon which he stood, and the speeches which he made. Probably he will be anxious to have us all forget how very far away he has got 'from the platform of 1919 which my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) showed us-[DOT] with the book closed-last night; he was very careful to make no reference to that platform, which all hon. gentlemen opposite seem to have got so far away from and of which the hon. leader of the Opposition is so thoroughly ashamed that when he comes to meet this House, not being able to reconcile the speeches for and the speeches against that platform which he has made on his tour, swaying from one side to the other as he passed from one constituency to another, that he simply takes refuge behind his amendment as if he were saying to himself: Well, as a result of all these things I have said, I have got the cards so hopelessly muddled that I do not think there is anything for it but to call for a new deal.

The Peterborough election also throws a light on the sincerity of this present clamour among hon. gentlemen opposite for an election. The hon. leader of the Opposition has said: The one thing necessary to the salvation of this country to-day is an election; I am here to turn out the Government for the sake of getting an election to-day. But what did he do when he learned that somebody with that doctrine as his sole doctrine, somebody willing "to put aside all questions of party differences had nailed to the mast the standard of an immediate election, and had gone out and asked the Peterborough electors to endorse his stand? Of course, this hon. gentleman, sincere believer in an immediate election as the one salvation of Canada, rallied to the support of that man. Of course he said: Shame on the man who talks party politics, shame on the man who would divide the people in the face of this supreme issue,-the one great object is to have an election to-day; gather your forces together, and let us, all who want a general election, vote together so that our votes may be effective. That is what you would expect if you did not know the leader of His Majesty's Opposition; but knowing the leader of His Majesty's Opposition, you were not disappointed when you saw him call for his horses and call for his men, and organize his party to go out and make war on the man who had ventured to say we ought to have an election. What a light that election throws on the sincerity of this .clamour for an election! This House is asked to say that the great paramount issue is an election or no election, that on its decision the salvation of this country, nay, perhaps more than that, the integrity of the British constitution depends. We on this side of the House who may in the past have belonged to different parties are appealed to to sink every consideration other than that, and vote in order that the country may be saved by a new election; and we are so asked by men fresh from the fray, glorying in their success over the man who preached the doctrine of an immediate election. I ask you now, how much faith can you put in the sincerity of this amendment?
I should hardly perhaps go back to them, because they are so insignificant, but the hon. member for Maisonneuve gave some considerations about the requisitioning of our ships during the war, about the cattle embargo, about the ships of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine carrying the

Canadian ensign, and about some difficulty with respect the the Gold Coast and Nigeria, all bearing upon our not being a nation.
As to the ships requisitioned in the war, the Canadian nation requisitioned her ships and put them at the service of the Allied nations, just as the Canadian nation sent her boys to fight for the common cause. I ask you in what respect that derogates from our national independence. As to the cattle embargo, I give that up. That you can find in the cattle embargo- that is, in one nation of this Empire, for its own protection, even as against other nations of the Empire putting on an embargo-any evidence that we are not distinct nations rather puzzles me. If anything, I should think it was evidence that we are distinct nations. Then we are asked, why do the vessels of the Canadian Government Merchant Marine now carry the Canadian ensign when the Niobe was not allowed to do so two years ago. I do not know it to be a fact, but I would say it is only a further evidence of the development to which I have pointed. We have privileges to-day that we did not have nine or ten years ago, and surely this only goes to show the development of our recognition as a nation. As to the Gold Coast and Nigeria, had the hon. gentleman paid attention he would have seen that in the item referring to the difficulty of, our directly negotiating with them, it was pointed out that Canada had outgrown these limitations which rest on the other parts of the Empire, but that Nigeria and the Gold Coast find themselves tied up, so it was not for any want of right on the part of Canada that we could not have gone on. It was, unfortunately, because the Gold Coast and Nigeria, being still Crown colonies, had no right to act on their own behalf. And the very item which the hon. gentleman read pointed out that fact. I have read to the House what Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier thought on this doctrine of mandates and the power of Parliament to deal with matters that had not been discussed at the general election. I may say that he made these observations in the course of a debate upon Reciprocity during which it did appear to hon. gentlemen then sitting on the other side of the House that there was need for a new election, because there was the proposal of a great new project in which was bound up not only the commercial but the national future of this country. It is
true that Sir Wilfrid Laurier ultimately gave an election, but he was careful to tell us in the speech he made, when the motion of closure was before the House, that he did not do so because our doctrine was right. He was very clear on that. He never flinched from the doctrine he laid down, but he told us that we should have the election because we had been naughty boys and had obstructed him. I do not want to express anything of a critical character on this point, but it did look a little like the case of the unjust judge of the Scriptures who yielded to the widow's insistence-not because she was right but because of her importunity. I merely wish to point this out in order that I may not be told that after all he did dissolve Parliament.
Now, in the course of his observations, the hon. member for Maisonneuve gave us several examples of what he considered to be deadly parallels, one of which was that of the Reciprocity debate and another, a parallel with some English election that occurred after the South African war. There, he pointed out, all of the contending parties opposed to the government came together- so differently from the way they did in Peterborough; if the parties here had taken the same course we might have begun to believe in the sincerity of those who are clamouring for a general election. In the meantime I only desire to call attention to the disparity between the two cases. We had another parallel, in which Mr. Asquith made a speech and talked about the policy of his adversaries as being one of zig-zag and-Oh, I have forgotten what else.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: See-saw.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. gentleman can tell me some of the others. Well, I listened to the hon. gentleman's remarks and then I thought of their application, and I could not help thinking of the clear-cut position taken in the speech from the Throne, and of the variegated policies of the leader of the Opposition and of the fact that, challenged to do it, he absolutely declines to tell us what definite policy, if any, he has. And then I wondered to whom the see-saw and the zig-zag applied. I am like the friend of Antonio in the play, who felt called upon to thank the Jew who had furnished him with the words which he wanted to use: "A very Daniel come to judgment" -a very see-saw and a very zig-zag! I wish the hon. gentleman would tell me the other adjectives, because they are so thor-

oughly applicable to the line of conduct of his own leader, a line of conduct in which the hon. gentleman apparently so complacently follows him. Mr. Speaker, I feel I should apologize for having devoted so much time in dealing with so small material. However, I have at last finished.
It is a gratification to me to be able, in my closing remarks, to join in one expression of opinion that fell from the lips of the hon. gentleman. He expressed the aspiration for unity among the people of this country. Let me say that in that hope I most heartily and most sincerely join; and I should be taking-no risks in saying that all hon. members on this side of the House endorse my sentiments. While we have duties with regard to the peace of the world, duties which we shall be able to perform, and while we have the duty of looking after the material interests of the people of this country, which come before any interests connected with the outside world, I am prepared to agree that we, all of us on both sides of the House, have one first great duty, and that is the duty of each trying to do his part to bring about and increase and preserve a feeling of unity between the different peoples of Canada. In making the eloquent appeal on this subject which he did, the hon. member for Maisonneuve did little more than re-echo the words of the Prime Minister of this Country as he uttered them first at Portage-la-Prairie, then in our good city of Sherbrooke, and also in our better city of Montreal, and as he has tried to send them broadcast throughout this country, extending his voice and hand, to greet every man, of whatever class, creed or political party, who is willing to join earnestly in the work of bringing about unity-observe, I do not say uniformity- among the people of this country I need not add anything to the eloquence of the hon. member for Maisonneuve further than to say that I join heartily in the hope he expressed in this respect. I might suggest to him, however, that he be good enough to have a heart to heart talk with some of the gentlemen who sit on. the same side of the House with him. I say this in no spirit of criticism, but perhaps to those hon. members he might point out acceptably, if I cannot, that it is not the best way of reaching unity to maintain the determination not to forget things that have happened in the past which largely, through misapprehension on one part or the other, have conduced to destroy the spirit of unity. One hon. gentleman the

other evening said he was prepared to forgive but not to forget. I would ask" him to think over a little what is the practical value of forgiveness on the part of one who continues to treasure up the memory of what he believes to be a wrong, and who, treasuring up that memory, seeks to keep alive the determination to have satisfaction for the wrong which he believes to have been inflicted. I am not here to plead in condonation of things that may have been wrong from one direction or another and which may have contributed to separate our people. But I am here in all honestly and sincerity to plead for a spirit all round of readiness to forget, asking only to ,be convinced that there is sincerity to-day in the desire to heal old wounds and to close up the gaps that have been created and that divide our people into different camps.
I appeal to gentlemen on this side as well as to gentlemen opposite to give thought to the necessity of the performance of that great duty of gathering together the Canadian people, and to give thought to what each of one of them may do, even if it involves the forgetting of some things, to bring about that most desirable end. As I have already said the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lemieux) in making an appeal for unity only re-echoed the words of the right hon. leader of the Government (Mr. Meighen) pronounced on different occasions and in different parts of this country. I have before me just a citation from his words on one occasion which I would like to give the House and with which I shall close these altogether too-prolonged observations. Speaking in the City of Montreal on the subjects to which the hon. gentleman referred, the Prime Minister said:
All I want is a fair field to show, in the practical task of government, that my desire to do something useful in the work of reconciliation is an honest desire, and that what I have already said I mean. Once more I' repeat that on this subject I am secure in one regard:	In all the years of my public life
I have uttered no words that now need to be recalled; nor have I ever been a party to a statute that in a single line was unfair to English or to French. All those who persist in attributing to me the language of prejudice or hostility have for seven months failed to produce a sentence from the record of twelve years to support the calumny and stand today as convicted perverters of the facts.
I am anxious for a fair distribution of the duties of Government. There is not such a fair distribution today, and my great anxiety is to be certain from week to week that I am not in the smallest degree responsible for a continuance of the unfairness that now exists.
I believe also in the fair distribution of public offices of ever}- kind, and I think that both the

great races' should recognize that a careful adherence to that principle is essential if we are ever going to get along. Such was the conviction and the practice of the best statesmen of the past, and we cannot forget their precepts now.
Here I leave the subject. Recalling the eloquent words of the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and calling attention to the equally eloquent words of my leader, I conclude with this appeal: That these words, this seed which they were intending to sow, may not fall upon barren ground but may produce four-fold and four times four-fold.
Let me in conclusion say that there will be one advantage at all events in the defeat of this amendment which I have no doubt will be reached within a few days, that it will afford the right hon. gentleman who leads the House the opportunity of proving the irrefutable truth that the words that he uttered were sincerely and absolutely meant. Let me further appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite to be fair, not to lend themselves to the keeping up of enmities and hostilities between our different races, our different peoples, and our different provinces, by attributing to the Prime Minister statements and sentiments which, at all events up to the present, nobody has been able to prove the existence of. I am confident that the people of the province of Quebec-whether they support him politically or are opposed to him-ere long will have the opportunity of realizing that in the present leader of this Government they have no enemy. I have known him since he first came into this House, and he has administered different offices always very closely under my eye. I remember with pride that he was my Solicitor-General and that for years-for some years at all events-I was his chief. I remember with pride now that he occupies to-day the position of my chief, and that I have the privilege and honour of following him. And let me pay him this testimony, as a mere measuring out of simple justice, that throughout my years of intimate relationship with him, I have never been able to discover any small feeling of bigotry, or prejudice, hostility or antipathy, to any class or creed within this Dominion; and above all I have never been able to discern the slightest indication of anything but the most friendly feeling and disposition to my old province of Quebec. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I fancy, will be fair enough to recognize that while they constitute the majority of the representatives from Quebec and while they
represent the majority of people of that province, that I too, and my colleague, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne), have a claim upon the same province. In our hearts there beats as strong an affection for that old province as exists in the heart of any hon. gentleman sitting opposite, and let me say that imbued with that feeling I would be in the government of no man that was inspired in the slightest degree by any spirit of hostility to the people and the province that I love.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you will be glad to know that it is not my intention to detain the House beyond a few minutes. The
5 p.m. speech from the Throne with which the session was opened is a beautiful negligible document. And that was to be expected. A Government which has outstayed its mandate and forfeited the confidence of the people, and which continues to cling to office in direct defiance of recognized public sentiment, is not likely to be one to originate or to initiate progressive and vigorous legislation. It is marking time; it is frightened to march forward, it is unwilling to make way. But, Sir, Canada is facing great questions of re-adjustment. There are big and pressing issues to be dealt with; yet if ever in the annals of government there has been an era of ineffective leadership it is at this present juncture. The speech from the Throne makes it abundantly clear that effective leadership cannot be expected from this disintegrated Unionist ministry. The Government has no policy to lay before the people in order to provide for the serious problem of increasing unemployment. The fulfilment of dismal prophecies made during the war has come with the icy blast of winter, and the problem of unemployment finds Canada unprepared. After the last two years of reconstruction the Government throws up its hands in despair, and appeals to the Provincial Governments and local municipalities to find a way out of the difficulty. What has become Mr. Speaker, of all these Commissions, of all these Boards of all sizes, complexions and descriptions that were so much in evidence? The Government has only been feeding parasites to make believe that they were taking steps and precautions in anticipation of the period of economic readjustment. Where are these gentlemen who personally conducted in this House excursions, unfolding to us the beautiful panorama of flaming fur-

naces, belching smoke-stacks, and happy men at work with full dinner pails? Instead we read the sad story that the dreaded spectre of the soup kitchen has made its appearance. Where is the distinguished gentleman whom we had the pleasure of seeing only twice in this House last session when he had been hurriedly despatched from Toronto headquarters to enrapture us with the delightful strain that, Liberalism meant panic and that Unionism meant prosperity? Why, Mr. Speaker, the last time that hon. gentleman was seen upon the floor of this House-and you remember the occasion?-he was trying to induce us to continue to remain bondsmen of Sir Joseph Flavelle and of Mackenzie and Mann. "Carry on! Carry on!" he said, those were his last words to the Government. That harp has since ceased its strain; and the Government has changed its name. Why, the truth is that-
The harp that once through Parliament's halls, The soul of prosperity music shed,
Now hangs as mute on Parliament's walls As if the nightingale from Leeds was dead.
But you have soup kitchens, and the burden is upon the hon. gentlemen opposite to explain the condition of thousands of men begging for work and of reduced wages to those fortunate enough to have employment. This is the melancholy of the acme of the "Carry on" administration.
This debate, Mr. Speaker, has been proceeding for a little time and charming things have been said. We have also witnessed the grotesque performance of a new self-constituted John the Baptist creeping into the National Liberal Conservative desert in search of grasshoppers to alleviate his treacherous hunger. Beautiful addresses also were delivered on the League of nations, or rather the League of Empires. To this subject, I desire to make a slight reference.
I understand very well that the - League which we were forced to approve of in this House could not leap full-grown into life, and I became convinced, after reading the speeches of our Canadian representatives which they recently delivered at Geneva, that the League must revise the Treaty or the Treaty will destroy the League. After hearing the addresses of the right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) and of the hon. gentleman from Durham (Mr. Rowell), although they eloquently stated that the League is to be the greatest forward movement in the world's history, yet it is plain to me that it contains the germ of future 
wars; and after hearing this afternoon the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), with his habitually lucid explanation, allow me to say, Sir, that the whole subject is darker than ever. The world is offered only an ideal. No word has been so misapplied in recent years as idealism. There is something splendid I grant you, in aspiring to the remote and the unattainable, providing it does not make us contemptuous of the slow steps towards better things that are attainable. But there are many kinds of idealists. Some like Darius Green, make themselves wings and mount to the ridgepole in a glow of aspiration, and leap out quick in the pleasant sunshiny air. But there are other idealists also, and they are of the kind I should like to see at Geneva, idealists more practical, who fashion their wings with due regard for the law of strains and stresses, who have a wholesome respect for the law of gravitation, and who will not mix trading stamps with moral issues. What is the use of sending men to Gevena to talk disarmament when on their return in their own Parliament by their votes they cheer the hearts of munition makers? Just so long as the big Powers who control the Supreme Council of the League retain all the important offices within the constructive programme of the League, and just so long as they will not agree to,disarmament, just so long as they will keep on mistrusting one another, just so long as they will refuse to forego national selfishness, the whole thing is-pardon me the expression, Mr. Speaker-"eye-wash."	Our representatives will only be enjoying a delightful trip at the expense of the Canadian people, just to have the pleasure of signing their names for Canada on the dotted lines already prepared for them, and the privilege of making speeches, which after all, to my mind, amounts to nothing. Sixty thousand Canadians walked their way to Golgotha and are now sleeping their last sleep on the fields of Flanders, and their actions, Sir, speak louder than all the speeches that can be delivered at Geneva by our representatives. They gave up their lives to end all wars, and what I should like to see, Sir, would be our representatives going to Geneva with a message from the Canadian people to the Supreme Council, which is the mouthpiece of the Great Powers, that they must agree to disarmament in order that Canada may remain true to her pledge to those who fought to end all war. Warmaking has been the sport of kings and

of sporty statesmen, not of the people. It has cost the sportiest kings their jobs, and the world is sick of sporty statesmen.
Sir, we have heard hon. gentlemen opposite offer a defence for their remaining in power. It has been plainly stated from this side of the House that the Government are carrying on without a mandate, and British practices and precedents have been quoted pro and con. I have this to say, Mr. Speaker:	This Tory Government and
its recent converts profess to find great merit in the so-called Unionist party, comparing it with the British coalition. But let jis not forget that in the Mother Country men of all parties formed a real union for the purposes of prosecuting the war. Here, where a different sense of political honour obtains, the combination has been made for the purpose of winning an election. In [DOT] England no one party accused the other of disloyalty; they did not make a pretence of friendly overtures in order to unite one section of the country against the other. They did not pass a Franchise Act by which they could control the elections. After the armistice there was an election in England; in Canada some of our Unionist gentlemen refuse to go to the people, keeping only their own selfish ends in view. I cannot make references to all these hon. gentlemen one after the other, but you will allow me, Mr. Speaker, to pay a little tribute to a gentleman from the prairies, that great Colossus of immigration. I well remember that on the first of May, 1917, the hon: gentleman gave an interview to a Saskatchewan paper with regard to the provision which has,been made for free wheat. He said: "Yes, it is great news, and we have to see to it that in the next Parliament we have free everything." At that time everything looked dark and gloomy for the Allied cause. I am not questioning the hon. gentleman's entry into the Cabinet in 1917, but he is the same gentleman who denounced the financial ring of Toronto, denounced the Borden Government as incompetent and retroactive, and denounced in no measured terms the government of "big business." I have said that I shall not comment upon the hon. gentleman's entry into the Cabinet in 1917. But, Sir, in his address in the House on the 11th of June, 1919, he said: "I say if I wanted to make a hero of myself, the road is quite clear to me." But he preferred to remain where he was. You remember, Sir, how tears ran down the cheeks of hon. gentleman when he deliberately sentenced himself to bread
crumbs and cold tea in the portfolio of Immigration. In his recent political tour of the West with the right hon. leader of the Government he said, as quoted from the prairies, that he had changed morally and mentally and that he had decided to spend eternity with the monopolists whom he had denounced all his life. Well, what idea can you have of the patriotism of a gentleman who can perform such a somersault?
I will not be as severe to him as he was to himself, but allow me to say of him that he was like Hosea Biglow's politician:
A marciful Providence fashioned him holler O' purpose that he might his principles smaller.
If that is a little too strong, Mr. Speaker,
I can give a better one. He at least believes, as Hosea did:
A genuine statesman must be on his guard.
If he must have beliefs, not to believe 'em too hard.
Bismarck used to say that Salisbury was a lath painted to look like iron. The hon. member from Moosejaw (Mr. Calder) is a Tory painted to look like a Liberal-he never was a Liberal; he posed as one. Like the coalitionists under Sir John A. Macdonald who refused to follow George Brown when he withdrew from the coalition, these hon. gentlemen have become reactionaries -makers of franchise Acts and gerrymander Acts.
Some hon. gentlemen have talked of apples and of the tariff, but, Sir, the issue before the House is the preservation of our constitutional treasures, our national heritage, which the Government is unscrupulously pawning every day without authority and without mandate. The issue is the disrespect of our laws, such as is involved in the building of a mercantile marine at a cost of $75,000,000, in connection with which contracts were awarded without tenders. The issue is the vicious railway policy of the Government, which is not established on a business foundation, and which makes the country responsible for the interest on millions of dollars' worth of obligations and deficiency in earnings. The issue is the lavish expenditures for militia purposes, amounting to eighteen or twenty millions of dollars, and the miserable pittance for eighteen small experimental farms. The issue is that the Government has created a paradise for its bosom friends, the profiteers, so that readjustment on a sane basis is practically impossible. The issue is that conscienceless rascals were permitted to accumulate outrageous profits and slip away with the spoils, leaving the business man behind holding the bag. The most discouraging

feature of the situation is that a spineless Department of Justice has made it impossible for the irresponsible shoe-string worker to be placed in such a position that he could be made to disgorge. The issue is the Government's scheme to deprive the people of their right to make any gradual political readjustment with due regard to economic conditions between 1911 and such time as they may choose.
Sir, a general election now would bring into Parliament no more representatives than at present, but it would open the door to the election of representatives who more closely reflect the vision of men who love freedom and hate autocracy.
The Prime Minister's extremist policy is calculated to dam the gradual flow of Canadian opinion and to interfere with the gradual process of parliamentary government. The last redistribution followed the census of 1911, and there was only one election on this redistribution, the wartime election of 1917. Enough has been said of this election that we need talk no more about it. No coalition candidate can pretend that he was elected on domestic issues, so that, excepting the 1917 election, no general election was held on this redistribution. Therefore, anyone voting against the amendment of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is only a party to the Prime Minister's scheme to thwart the will of the people, to carry parliament through 1911 to 1922, and such men should be known to their constituents as men who refuse to face an election because they know they have lost the confidence of the electorate. I am not afraid to go before my constituents, to meet my judges.
I heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) say, during his long address this afternoon, that the Government had a moral issue, Moral issue! Eternal issue! Give us an opportunity to meet the Knights of Morality. Speaking for my constituents and myself, we have had to endure many things during the last years. Dr. Crane used to say that, in this world one cannot get what he wants, without getting a whole lot of truck he does not want. Desires may be pure and unmixed, but the gratification thereof is spotted. We have thrown on the shores of time all the truck we do not want. We forgive everything; but we do not forget and will never forget the rampant super-loyalty, pathetically stupid, of the junkers of the last election, whose delight it was to pillory the French Canadians as a body, and who have committed the worst political crime in Canada's his-

tory. We will not put on the shelves of oblivion the malignity with which the loyalty and patriotism of that great Canadian and Empire builder, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and the rank and file of the Liberal party, were openly and maliciously assailed in such terms as " traitor," " disloyal," " yellow-back," " quitter," " pro-German," -all that to win a party triumph. To us this crime and sin against the nation has struck deep and far, and every true patriot to-day, now that the storm of rancour and abuse is over, contemplates with dismay and horror the national wreckage wrought by fire-eaters and reactionaries. We will remember the mischief that those impudent junkers have done by their uncalled-for, and unreasoning and unreasonable " namecalling " of men and women whose character, citizenship, loyalty and patriotism ring as true as steel, and whose only offence was that of differing with those super-heated patriots in regard to the way in which Canada should have taken her part in the war. We hope now that when the junkers' temperature goes down to normal, they will have the saving grace and the redeeming quality of commonsense that will make plain to them the assinine exhibition that they have made of themselves and what a terrible wound they have inflicted on our national unity. Laurier's life-work of Canadian unification has been demolished, and to heal the wound, to mend the breach that has been produced by stupidity stampeded by bigotry and fanaticism, there is only one remedy-an immediate appeal to the people. This is the humble prayer of the electors of Bellechasse, which I, their humble representative, wish to lay at the foot of your Throne.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate my hon. friend, who has just spoken, on having had delegated to him the important task of informing this House what the issues are which the Opposition propose to lay before the people at the next general election, in the near future, if they succeed -as is very unlikely-in securing a favourable vote on this amendment? We have had a debate lasting now for one week, and this is the first time that the House has heard any of the issues which the Opposition party proposes to lay before the electors of the country. I have not hitherto obtruded myself to any great extent upon the time of this House; but I feel that the amendment now before you, with its result one way or the other, is so important that I shall depart from my usual custom of

registering a silent vote; and I am impelled to give some reasons why I oppose the amendment.
Before doing so, I should like to add my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the address. It is generally conceded that the speeches of the mover and the seconder of the address in reply are of a very high order, and it will be admitted that the speeches made this session have not fallen below the standard which is usually expected on such occasions. More particularly would I like to congratulate, and I am pleased to be able to do so, the seconder, not because I would wish to make any comparison between the two speeches, but because he is a gentleman whom I have known for many years and because he represents a constituency adjoining mine, which he and I have seen develop from almost nothing to its present wonderful state of production. It was his maiden effort in this House, on the second day of his membership, and I think that the majority of the members will agree with me in concluding that his constituents have made no error of judgment in selecting him as their representative, and that he is one of whom they have reason to be proud.
Mr. Speaker, I have read over the amendment proposed by the leader of the Opposition, and I find that it contains three assertions. With these I should like to deal. His first assertion is that the present Government does not possess the confidence of this House. I do not think it is necessary for me to take up any time with regard to that assertion because it is one that can only be tested by the vote which will be taken at the close of this debate. The vote will show whether or not the present Government possesses the confidence of this House. '
His second assertion is that the Government does not possess the confidence of the country, and his third assertion that the retention of office by the Government constitutes a usurpation of the powers of popular Government. Dealing with the second assertion, the leader of the Opposition tried to prove it by two arguments. His first point was that he made that statement on the strength of the results of the by-elections which have taken place since December 1917. That point has already been dealt with fully by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Justice, and I do not propose to add anything to what they have said, except this:	Out of
the six seats which the leader of the
Opposition states the Government has lost, there is only one in which a candidate running as one of) the Liberal Opposition party has been returned, and in his case it would appear that the platform on which he presented himself to the electors of his constituency was not the platform of the Liberal party, but one of his own. The second point which the leader of the Opposition endeavoured to make was that he made that assertion as a result of his personal observation.	Now I have not had the
opportunity Which	he has had (of
observing the feeling of the people or this country from the Atlantic to the Pacific, for he has made a tour of the country, but I must say that I think I can better judge the feelings of the people of my own constituency than can the leader of the Opposition, and so far as my constituency is concerned, so far as my observation goes, I do not think his assertion is correct. ' If that is so, I think his assertion cannot be relied upon with respect to the whole country. I have yet to have a single Liberal who supported me in the general election of 1917, and there were many 6f them, come to me and intimate that he thought after the termination of the war I should resign my seat, or that he thought the Government should resign. Again, as in the case of the first assertion, the truth can only be tested by a general election itself. When we get that, we shall know whether or not the assertion is true and not until then.
The third assertion is that the Government has usurped the powers of popular government. That, to my mind, Mr. Speaker, is the most important assertion of the three and probably the only one which contains any element of danger for the Government. I say it contains an element of danger for this reason. The people of any democratic country will resent most strongly anything of that kind, any attempt on the part of the Government of the country to usurp the powers of popular government. They will stand for almost anything rather than that. But, as the Minister of Justice has said, if a statement is made frequently enough, in the end it will probably come to be believed, not only by the person who makes it, but by some of those who hear it; and there is the danger. This is an assertion which has been made on every platform on which the leader of the Opposition has spoken during the last two months. It is an insidious statement because it is one which, if believed in, will

be most strongly resented by the electors of the country. What grounds has the leader of the Opposition or any hon. gentleman opposite for making any such assertion? What are the facts? What are the arguments which they bring forward in support of their fact?
Their premises are that the Union Government was elected solely for the purpose of dealing with the war, that that was the only issue in the election of 1917. I grant, Mr. Speaker, that it was the main issue, but I do not grant that it was the only issue. We have in every general election some main issue, some issue that is singled out and on which as a matter of fact the whole election is really fought. It is certainly true that in the election of 1917 the main issue, the one outstanding and overshadowing issue, was that of the prosecution of the war, and in comparison with that all other questions faded into insignificance. But when the statement is made that that was the only issue, I think I need only refer to the manifesto which was published, containing the line of policy which would be followed by the Union Government if returned to power. That manifesto contained twelve planks. I have a copy before me and I find that of those twelve not more than two or possibly three are confined to matters relating to the war. The others are all matters that apply equally to times of peace as to the period of the war. Many of them do not even refer to problems that arise out of the war. For example, take the second, Civil Service Reform. That has nothing to do with the war or the prosecution of the war; the third, the Extension of the Franchise to Women; the fifth, A Strong Progressive Policy of Immigration and Colonization; the seventh, Development of Transportation Facilities; eighth, Reduction of Public Expenditure; tenth, Encouragement of Co-operation among those engaged in Agricultural Production; eleventh, General Development of all the Varied Resources of Canada; and twelfth, Adequate Consideration of the Needs of the Industrial Population. The great majority of these planks are matters that have no reference to the war. I contend that when this platform was before the electors of Canada, every one of its planks was submitted to their consideration and approval; and while under the' circumstances existing at that time every person's mind and attention was directed almost solely to the great issue of the war and these other planks may have been tem-	-
porarily forgotten in the larger importance of the other, nevertheless they were all there as a part of the policy of the Union Government. And if any mandate was given to that Government it was, as the Minister of Justice has pointed out, given by the people of Canada to their representatives for the purpose of being acted upon; each representative elected in support of the Unionist Government was given a mandate to support the carrying out of every plank of that platform. The war has terminated successfully; I do not think many of us expected that it would end as quickly as it did when the election was in progress. But there are still problems arising out of the war, some of which were mentioned in that platform and which are still being dealt with. There are many-other planks which, as I have said, have no reference to the war or to after-war problems and which are not yet fully dealt with. Therefore, I say that the mandate of the Government is not exhausted.
The point is made that the personnel of the Government is different; and the leader of the Opposition named twelve out of the original members of the Government who are no longer in that Government. I have looked over the list and find that of the twelve one was defeated in the general election, two are dead, two have fbeen appointed to office, and seven are still in the House; and so far as ocular evidence goes, only two of those are on the other side of the House, the other five still giving strong support to this Government.
What about the constitutional right of the Government to carry on? I do not think that point need be laboured. The leader of the Opposition and the Opposition members must, I think, concede that as a matter of right this Government is entitled to carry on. But they say that they have no moral right to do so. As to the constitutional right, so far as I am aware, no question could be raised if, in the event of the Government being defeated and the leader of the Opposition being called upon, he should carry on in this House for the term of this Parliament, if he chose to do so and could find sufficient support in the House. That has been done in the British Parliament on several occasions, the last occasion, if I remember rightly, being in the year 1885 when the Government of Mr. Gladstone was d'-feated. Although he had a large majority in the House he was defeated on a chance vote, and Lord Salisbury took office after considerable hesitation and carried on for some months before asking for dissolution.

It was done in our own country in the province of British Columbia. In 1903 when the Prior Government was defeated and Mr. McBride was called upon to form a Government, he completed the work of the House and passed the Estimates before dissolving. Precedents have been quoted, and it is said that this is not the same Government. Well, was the Government in Great Britain the same in 1915 as the one which took office in 1911 or 1910? In that election, if my memory serves me rightly, Campbell-Bannerman was returned, succeeded by Mr. Asquith. At the outbreak of the war a Coalition Government was formed entirely different from that which was returned to power at the general election; but there was no special mandate from the people to that Government to continue. In 1915 Mr. Lloyd George succeeded Mr. Asquith and made further changes, and that Government which carried on there until 1918 was as different as it possibly could be from the Government returned to power in 1919.
I should like to state a supposititous case-one very difficult, indeed, to suppose. But let us assume for the purpose of argument that the election in 1917 had resulted differently and that the Union Government had been defeated and the Liberal party returned to power. Their argument is that the people in that election had only in contemplation the question of the war, and had only in contemplation that whatever Government was returned to power should only carry * on until the termination of the war. In that supposititous case, had the Liberal party been returned, I wonder would they have admitted at the termination of the war that their mandate was exhausted, and that they should dissolve and go to the country.
