speechtext:
Can you, Mr. Speaker,
by any stretch of imagination conceive of the Liberal party admitting what they are now arguing against this Government? The argument surely cuts both ways, and if it holds good against the present Government it certainly ought to hold good in the case which I have just mentioned.
To my mind, an unfortunate allusion was made by both the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux), the allusion to the conduct of the Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1911, which was referred to by both these speakers but in a very different manner. The leader of. the Opposition in dealing
with the point would rather lead one to infer that in the session of 1911 no mention was made of the reciprocity question. He stated in his speech that Sir Wilfrid Laurier recognized the rights of the people as superior to those afforded his Government under the Constitution; he believed that governments should be carried on only with the consent of the governed. He dissolved Parliament and appealed to the people to pass upon an issue other than which was involved in the elections of 1908. My hon. friend made no reference whatever to the fact that the reciprocity resolution was introduced into the House in 1911? The member for Maisonneuve dealt with the matter in a different manner. He stated the facts. He stated that the resolutions were introduced, but that the Opposition strenuously opposed them, and as a result of that opposition the Government went to the country. I believe those are the facts. But the member for Maisonneuve, I submit, was wrong in his argument in this respect. He said that reciprocity was no new issue and that it had been before the country on previous occasions. So it had been. But what was the result when the issue was before the country on those occasions? Did the country accept the principle? The country had rejected on all previous occasions any attempt at reciprocity. Now it was no issue in 1908 at the general election, and yet the leader of the Government in 1911 introduced no new principle, as the member for Maisonneuve says, but brought in the reciprocity resolutions against all previous decisions of the electors of this country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose I was referring to the reciprocity resolutions introduced in the session of 1911. Perhaps I may be pardoned if, for the sake of picking up the thread of my argument, I am guilty of a little repetition. I stated that this question was referred to, both by the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), and I stated further that each dealt with it in an entirely different manner.
If we are to accept the argument of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, a Government has the right to introduce and to en-

his food, and for all the necessities of life. Find work for them. Why not start immediately and build the Georgian Bay canal? This is a national undertaking, one which would be of advantage to the country, while workmen would earn fair wages. All important public bodies are clamouring for the building of this canal. The Boards of Trade of Montreal and of Hull have both passed resolutions requesting the Government to have this work carried out immediately, but they have only met with refusals, the Minister of Finance stating that he was without funds for such an undertaking, the public revenue having been absorbed in paying interest on the war debt.
I am well aware, Mr. Speaker, that our national debt exceeds two billions; nevertheless, millions have been found for the purchase of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk; the operations of the first year have left a deficit of $60,000,000. The expenses of the militia have been increased by six millions yearly, though the war is over and we do not need a militia. The hon. Minister of Marine intends spending millions on a navy which is not necessary in peace time. This reply that there is no money is but an excuse, Mr. Speaker. Money can always be found to help large firms, or to enrich political friends; yet, there is none for an undertaking which would further the development of the country, while the farmer would be afforded greater facilities for the shipment of his products and the labourer would be supplied with work.
I also note, in the speech from the Throne, that the Government intends considering the opportunity of paying old age pensions and protect the labourer from unemployment. I would be tempted to rejoice, Mr. Speaker, because, at every session, since I have the honour-of sitting in this House, I have requested that such legislation be passed in favour of the workmen. My. only fear is that it is but a false hope, that the Government will content themselves with an investigation, without legislating on the matter. As I have said in previous years, when a man has spent all his life in enriching his master,-the man, very often having but insufficient wages to support his own family,-it is not fair that he should be compelled, when too old to work, either to go to the poorhouse, or be left a charge to his children. The Government should, I think, establish a pension fund for these old employees.
I would also mention, Mr. Speaker, the compliments and the loud praise given to

the Province of Quebec by my hon. friend who seconded the address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. I quite realize that this is a serious moment for the Government, that their only chance of remaining in power is by making friends in the province of Quebec. But, Sir, allow me to say that it requires more than mere words to make us forget all the abuse and the insults that were heaped on us during the war. I remember that, in 1917, the press and the Tories, headed by Mr. Meighen, endeavoured to rouse the English provinces against Quebec; now that Quebec may be of help, compliments are being bestowed upon her. In so far as I am concerned, and quite contrary to my hon. friend from St. Hyacinthe (Mr. L. J. Gauthier), I am as indifferent to their compliments as I am to their insults, and will have no faith in those fine words until our share of patronage has, in all justice, been given us, either in the Cabinet, or in the several commissions, or yet in the public appointments that may be made, and until the French language has been given the place of honour to which it is entitled in Parliament and throughout the country.
Before concluding these remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state that I am in favour of the amendment moved by the honourable leader of the Opposition, and I shall ask all the members of this House, especially those who are sitting on your right, Sir, to act independently; let them heed the voice of their conscience which tells them that the Government's mandate has expired, that they are only usurpers, that they should vote in favour of the amendment of the leader of the Opposition, so that we may have elections immediately.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is customary on the occasion of the debate on the Address in reply to the speech from the Throne for this House to pass in review the programme that the Government submits in that speech through the lips of His Excellency the Governor General and the record and activities of the Government during the preceding months or years. But in this case, Sir, it would appear that the ancient custom has been almost wholly departed from. Immediately following upon the two excellent speeches delivered by the mover (Mr. Mclsaac) and the seconder (Mr. Mac-Kelvie) of the Address, the hon. leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) introduces an amendment which, I think, in the eyes of all thoughtful members of this

House can be construed as nothing less than a straight negative of the resolution.
This amendment, which has been characterized as a bald amendment-and I think it is properly so named-has been very largely the subject of debate. Were we called upon to deal with the amendment in itself we could very well afford to dismiss it with but a few observations. But my hon. friends opposite, more particularly the leader of the Opposition, have, during the course of their arguments, made a great many statements and assertions and offered certain condemnations in regard to the Government, which, I think, call for some attention on the part of members on this side. It is because of this that I propose to deal with the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite rather than specifically and solely with the subject matter contained in the resolution and in the amendment.
We find the Government faced with two oppositions, two groups of hon. gentlemen in this House representing certain policies. At least, these two groups have given to the public two distinct policies, though in one sense we find them apparently united. I have been waiting for a week to hear from the hon. gentleman sitting at the end of the Chamber and to obtain a lead as to their views, but judging from reports I think I am not mis-stating it when I say that they are apparently united in opposition to the Government in regard to this question.
Now, I wish to direct the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to certain facts, and in doing so I desire also to appeal to them, because I am quite certain that the majority of them, while they may appear on the surface to be more or less blindly following their leaders, are most anxious to weigh matters carefully and to give due consideration to arguments that may be advanced. My hon. friends who represent the Liberal party in this House present a certain view. I do not see the leader of the Opposition in his seat; if he were here I would ask him to correct me if I mis-state the position they take. In his absence I will ask my hon. and genial friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) to do so. Their position, I think, may be summed up in this way: they assert that the Government has lost the confidence of this House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am happy, Sir, to know that I have not mis-stated their position; I will come to that a little later. I will make a further statement now, in which I shall endeavour to interpret the arguments they have advanced and the position they have assumed. They assert in most violent language that the Government has lost the confidence of the country.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am again most happy in having correctly stated their position. Indeed, Sir, I have before me the words of the leader of the Opposition in which he says that we should have an election at once. I do not wish to quote his remarks at any length, but this was his statement in support of his amendment a few days ago. I turn to my hon. friends, and I do not wish to characterize them as the North-East Party:	I will characterize them in the
term that they prefer, the Agrarian party, and I do that for the purpose of distinguishing them from my hon. friends immediately opposite. They have a slightly different position. So far as I have been able to gather from the published statements of their leaders, they assert that they do not want an election forthwith; but they say: "Inasmuch as last year or on a previous occasion we joined in a vote of want of confidence, we think it would be desirable for us to join in this vote of want of confidence, because we have no apprehension that the Government will be defeated or that an election will be brought on, but we shall be in this safe position of having said that we have no confidence in the Government." I hear no objection to that, and I once again assume that I am not misstating the fact or the case. I want to invite my hon. friends to consider this matter. In his most recent public utterances, utterances made under conditions under which we are warranted at least in assuming that he was expressing his innermost thoughts-and that was in the late byelection in Peterborough-the leader of the Opposition had this to say, and I invite most careful consideration to these words:
From now until the day of a general election only one of two things can possibly happen. Either the Meighen Administration will continue to hold power or it will be defeated on a vote of want of confidence-
That is a plain statement. Then he added these significant words:
m which event it would be the duty-
Mark you.
-of His Excellency the Governor General to call upon the leader of the Opposition to form an administration.

In this House the leader of the Opposition has been thundering in the interest of the people. In his statement which I have quoted, he says this: "It is not a general election that I want; it is simply that the Meighen Government"-I am using his own words, and in doing so I am not violating the rules of the House-"shall be defeated, and I, as leader of the Opposition, shall be called upon to form a Government." In other words, he has let the cat out of the bag. The sole incentive, objective,, on the part of the hon. gentleman leading the Opposition is accession to office. My hon. friends will have great difficulty in escaping from that position because, before I get through, I am going to offer them a way out which I am quite certain they will not accept. I turn to my hon. friends of the Agrarian party, composed very largely of hon. gentlemen from the three Prairie Provinces-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
From all over the
place.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I said "very largely;" I will very willingly include hon. gentlemen from other parts of Canada. I say the group very largely composed of hon. gentlemen from the Prairie Provinces, and great credit to them. This is the position in which they will find themselves. In supporting this amendment and admitting that they are sincere in that support, if they succeed in defeating the Government, they can have no redistribution before a general election. I am a member from the province furthest west, and I claim in this House, on behalf of and in the name of my province, this right, that there should be a redistribution before a general election so that my province may have its proper representation in this House. That is a very important point in this matter.
Indeed, were it not for the fact of a redistribution coming on, or that a redistribution should occur before a general election, I would not have any very great objection to the demands of my hon. friends opposite for an election. I would welcome it; but as a representative of a British Columbia constituency which has grown very largely, and from a province which, I believe will have a larger representation in the new House than in this, I claim that as a right, and I say that right is of very great importance. I say to my hon. friends from the three Prairie Provinces-and I invite their attention to this with all seriousness and earnestness, that there are

peculiar to Western Canada problems apart from politics, apart from our party or their party, which will never be solved until the West has a very much larger representation than it has now, and it is our duty, if we are true to the interests of our particular section of the country, that that increase of representation in this House should be brought about at the earliest possible date.
I will give one illustration, and I will not labour the point, because this is not the time to do so. I will bring it to the remembrance of my hon. friends that for ten years I have on frequent occasions brought to the attention of the House, as it has been brought to the attention of the proper legal authorities, namely, the Railway Commission, the inequality in freight rates in this country. This is an important problem to which I have given exhaustive study. When I state that in my province and in some parts of the prairies we are paying a freight rate, in most cases, approximately three times the charge in Eastern Canada, it will be recognized that we have a grievance. That is a grievance that has no political aspect, that can be solved, as my hon. friends know, only by proper and weighty representation in this House, and there are many other problems of equal importance. What I wish to say to them is this-and I am not now talking for the sake of argument of a political character-British Columbia and the three Prairie Provinces are the only provinces in Canada that stand to gain by a Redistribution Bill, and I stand here to claim for British Columbia-and I hope my hon. friends from the Prairie Provinces will claim the same for their provinces- the fulfilment of that right of representation in this House.
I wish to deal with one other phase of that question before I leave it, because it will be advanced no doubt by those who seek excuses for a position opposite to the one I am suggesting. It has already been intimated in the press that hon. gentlemen will argue that any increased representation will accrue to the cities; that it will not accrue to the rural districts. Be that as it may, in the first place, I am not going to argue vainly that the Prime Minister and his Government and hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will deal fairly and honestly with the Redistribution Bill, because if hon. gentlemen opposite ' have made up their minds to the contrary, nothing I say will convince them. But assuming for the sake of argument that the cities will gain, have not the

cities a right to gain if they have the necessary population?
Take my own city, for instance. We have heard throughout the length and breadth of this land as one of the basic cries backing up the Red interests in this country, that the labour interests have not got fair representation. Now, if you give increased representation to the cities, does not labour get a larger opportunity? Undoubtedly it does, because labour controls the vote in the cities, absolutely controls it. So I invite my hon. friends to the consideration of this point: If it does turn out that the cities will gain under the Redistribution Bill, is it not right that they should gain, providing they have the necessary population? I say to my hon. friends, that before they commit themselves irrevocably to this vote of want of confidence demanding, as it does, in the words of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, an immediate election, they must give it careful consideration and be prepared to face the western section of this country and explain why they voted against the proper representation of the West in this House.
Let me turn now to another phase of this question. Has there been any general demand in this country for a general Election? Outside of the pilgrimage undertaken by the leader of the Opposition, who at every place he spoke dwelt on this subject of improper representation in this House, and sought to disseminate throughout the country mistrust of Parliament- not of the Government, but of Parliament -there has been no utterance on the subject by any outstanding citizen, or any groups of citizens, so far as I know, with the exception of one group.
You know, Mr. Speaker, as do all hon. gentlemen who have been in this House some years, that one of the readiest ways ox presenting a demand to this House is by means of telegrams, letters, petitions, and so forth. How often, Sir, we have sat in this House and seen hon. gentlemen rise in their place when the Orders of the Day were called, and proceed to read telegrams about this, that and the other thing in condemnation of the Government. Do you think that if such a demand existed, if it had been expressed by any large body of citizens, we would not have heard of it? Have you seen anything of it in the press? Has there been a single board of trade from one end of Canada to the other that has made such a demand? Have we had any such demand from labour organizations? Have we had any such demand from municipal or civic governments in this country, or from Provincial Legislatures? You might ask why I cite them.
I do so for this reason: We have been told here, not once, but scores of times, that we are usurping the people's rights.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friends opposite say "hear, hear." I would ask them how can we usurp the people's rights without infringing upon the inherent and constitutional rights of municipal and provincial governments, and the activities of commercial bodies? Can we do so? And has there been a single representation from any of these bodies to this House or to the public? Absolutely none. Again I repeat, the only demand for a general election originates with and comes from my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, whose sole object is the attainment of office in this country.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the War Veterans?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I forgot to mention
them. I intended to say that I did hear of a demand from one quarter, and it was this. Mr. Harry Flynn, a gentleman whom I think nearly everybody in this House knows, and who requires no introductory remarks from me, held a meeting in Vancouver, a portion of which city I represent, and under the influence of his eloquence a resolution was passed demanding that this Government immediately go to the country. Outside of that, Sir, I have seen nothing, and \ know of nothing, in the way of a demand for a general election.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: What about the Peterborough by-election?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend is going to hear something about the Peterborough by-election in a minute. What about the Peterborough by-election? We might as well talk about it now as later. The Peterborough by-election showed this that there was a Liberal candidate in the field, the first and only one in the five byelections since the right hon. the leader of the Government took office. That Liberal Candidate got a minority vote of the electorate of Peterborough by virtue of the fact that the Government support was divided into two, although it polled a larger vote than was accorded the Liberal candidate. There was two other candidates in the field, one representing the Farmers, and one representing Labour. My hon. friend's

candidate will enter this House in a few days, and will no doubt be received with roars of applause by hon. gentlemen opposite, although representing but a very small minority of the people of Peterborough. I have no objection to that, because he is constitutionally elected and entitled to his seat. If my hon. friends opposite can get any comfort out of that, they are entitled to it, but there is mighty little comfort in it.
Why did they not run a candidate in Yale? Why did they not run a candidate in Colchester? What about St. Jolfn? They abandoned their poor candidate down there. What about the splendid run made by my hon. friend's candidate in Elgin? Why, not long ago the leader of the Opposition made a speech in Peterborough in which he pointed to the drubbing the Government's candidate got in Elgin. As a matter of fact, Sir, we lost by about 200 votes. My hon. friend did not say anything about the drubbing his candidate got. He lost by about 2,000 votes. My hon. friend asks me what about Peterborough? I ask him, what about these other four ridings? If he can get any consolation out of having a minority candidate squeezed in, out of five candidates, in Peterborough he is welcome to it.
I was proceeding to ask: have not all the reasons that have been advanced here in support of this amendment existed since the armistice was signed? There have been three sessions prior to this since the armistice was signed-the spring of 1919, the fall of 1919, and the 1920 session, and yet this is the first occasion since the armistice was signed that my hon. friends have raised the question of a direct want of confidence vote. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) did, it is true, introduce resolutions which I shall deal with a little later on in connection with another subject. They were resolutions dealing with a specific and stated reason why there should be a want of confidence-an amendment to the Budget-but there was not a word in them such as is contained in the amendment now under consideration.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, there was.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Not a word, and I defy the hon. gentleman to produce it.
As a matter of fact, their attitude to-day vindicates the Government up to this time in their own eyes. By their attitude today they virtually give the Government a

clean bill of health for the last three years. Now, I have another statement which I desire to make, and I am going to quote very briefly from the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King). He says that the will of the people has been ignored. I observe that my hon. friends are not applauding now. They applauded pretty vigorously a while ago, but it seems that they are becoming rather dubious of the wisdom of the stand taken by their leader. That hon. gentleman also said that the rights of the people were usurped.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They got it this time. The rights of the people, says the hon. gentleman, have been usurped-by whom? By this parliament.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, by the government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Were hon. members
opposite not elected on exactly the same franchise as hon. members on this side?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No? Do I hear hon.
members say "no"? My hon. friend from I.unenburg (Mr. Duff) does not invite me, surely, to analyze the election in Lunenburg?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I repeat
what I have already said, that hon. gentlemen opposite were elected to this parliament on the same basis as that on which hon. gentlemen on this side were returned. They were elected under the same franchise. Now, they tell us that the rights of the people have been usurped by parliament, for that is the logical inference.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am glad to get confirmation from my hon. friend from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon), an hon. member who, I think, understands constitutional law very well, and who can speak with authority on the subject. It has been stated here that the Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Meighen) has lost the confidence of this House; and that even if he has nor lost the confidence of the House he has no right to hold office, because he has usurped the rights of the people.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Sure.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I think I am stating
their argument fairly. Now, I say this to everyone of them, that if they are convinced that they are accurate and true in that

statement; if they are behind the leader of the Opposition in his various assertions, of which I shall give samples in a moment, then there is a very easy and simple way of remedying the trouble. What is it? A very short time ago-last session, I think, or the session before-through the initative of my hon. friend from Montreal-I have forgotten the exact riding-a Bill was passed in this House making it imperative that a by-election should be held within six months. Am I not right? I certainly am. My hon. friends last July, when the House prorogued, knew that it was improperly constituted, as they say; well, knowing now that the government has usurped the rights of the people; knowing that the franchise was, to use their own language, a piece of public debauchery; knowing all these things and being convinced, as they say they are, why do not they not resign their seats and appeal to the people?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Because the Government would rob the treasury.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friends laugh but I challenge them to consider this point. Do they mean to say, believing that, that if hon. gentlemen vacated their seats the Government would dare to carry on? In any case, if they had taken this step before the House was called together we would have had a miniature general election even if the Government had continued to hold office, for we would have had to run a by-election in every seat. But in order to safeguard the treasury, which some hon. gentleman evidently fears might suffer, why could they not divide their forces, leaving one valiant band in this House to watch the Government, and allowing the other noble band of patriots to appeal to the country? Then we should have a pretty good test of public opinion. But my hon. friends know that if a large number of their members-not all, but a large number-thought for' one moment that there was any danger of the Government being defeated and a general election being brought on immediately they would not support the amendment but would rather support the Government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Try it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friends cannot escape the position in which they have placed themselves. They have reiterated time and time again in this House that this Parliament is improperly constituted. If, however, it is properly constituted and
the Government have the confidence of Parliament the constitutional argument of my hon. friends is gone to the winds; there is no argument. My hon. friends cannot escape the position in which they find themselves. By their own admission, and by the statements of their own leader, the case is proved against them.
But they do not rest there. They take care to go further and insinuate into the minds of the people that in some way or other Parliament is not properly constituted. I purpose for a moment to meet them frankly on one of their charges. My hon. friends have used the word "debauchery" pretty freely in this debate in referring to the War-time Elections Act and the election of hon. members to this House. It is a rather serious charge, and if it is made with any degree of sincerity it is one that challenges the attention of Parliament. Let me say to my hon. friends that so far as I am concerned I am prepared to discuss the War-time Elections Act as it was applied to the elections that I know anything about anywhere in the country. I know how it was applied in British Columbia and in the West. I do not think there is an hon. gentleman sitting in this House, either of the Agrarian party elected under that Act or any of my friends from the western provinces sitting on this side, who was elected in any way except with the clearest expression of public opinion which any parliamentarian has ever received since Confederation.
What were the iniquitious features of the Act? Here they are: We gave the soldiers overseas the vote; that was one. We enlarged the franchise by giving the vote to women who had relatives overseas. Why did we not go further? I am going to state frankly, on my own responsibility entirely, one of the reasons which appeal to me, and it is this: While we were in the throes of war it was not common sense, it was not wise, in deed it would have been exceedingly ill-advised had we given the franchise to persons of alien enemy origin in this country. There is no use closing our eyes to that fact. The hon. leader of the Opposition, in speeches he has made all over this country, says that a large section of the community were disfranchised. Now, whom did we disfranchise? We disfranchised only that section of the community to which I have just referred, and I say that were a similar condition to face us again to-day we could not do otherwise. And so I say to my hon. friends, when they use the word "de-
21S

J
bauchery" in connection with the 1917 elections, I think they are exceeding the bounds of reason and ordinary consideration for the interests of the country.
Now let me proceed to another phase of this question. I want to say a few words in connection with the tariff. We are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that the tariff should not be introduced in this discussion, that we should not obtrude upon this debate the question of the fiscal policy of the country. Sir, I was in the West Peterborough election. That constituency was my old home. I spent my boyhood years there, and I witnessed the recent campaign. I can quote the platform of the candidates -the candidate of my hon. friends opposite and the Agrarian candidate-and a very large portion of their platform was taken up with utterances on the tariff-a very large portion of it.
The leader of the Opposition, in his speeches there, made a very definite statement, and I invite the attention of the House not only to the statement he made in Peterborough, but to the statement he made in Kamloops on his western trip, and to the platform which he no doubt had a considerable part in drawing. Then I invite the House to the consideration of this: After viewing these various statements made by the leader of the Opposition it is easy to understand why he does not want the subject discussed in this House. The one thing my hon. friend wants to escape is the tariff, or a fiscal policy, as an issue in this country. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), who is not now in his seat, the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), and other hon. gentlemen from the great industrial provinces of Quebec and Ontario-imagine these hon. gentlemen forced to get in behind a platform such as we have here in The message from Liberalism in the records of the 1919 convention in this city. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) nods his head in approval when I mention it. I give him credit at least for being consistent. He stands by this policy. My hon. friend would move the adoption of this policy, if his colleagues would allow him to move it and if he had the opportunity, to-morrow. Before this session is over my hon. friend will tell the House that he stands by every item in that tariff platform. He certainly will. On the other hand, the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens, the hon. member for North Cape Breton, the hon. member for

Maisonneuve, and a score of others, will advocate something that is absolutely contrary to the principle. I challenge them to make this question an issue in the next election. They will not do it, they dare not do it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The record of the Government.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That was a pretty faint ''hear, hear," Mr. Speaker; they are not very enthusiastic about this. Let me continue with the quotation:
That a revision downwards of the tariff should be made whereby substantial reductions should be effected in the duties on wearing apparel and footwear, and on other articles of general consumption (other than luxuries), as well as on the raw material entering into the manufacture of the same.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
A very earnest "hear, hear," from the Agrarian party but a very sporadic expression from the Liberal Opposition. But, Mr. Speaker, having read what I have I invite you to listen to this:
And the Liberal Party hereby pledges itself-
You can just imagine the solemnity of the occasion when this was read and affirmed

by those at the convention with their hands raised to heaven.
And the Liberal Party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provision of this resolution when returned to power.
Some hon. GENTLEMEN: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Why do not my hon. friends make a decent parliamentary, constitutional attempt to implement their pledges by moving that as an amendment?
I challenge them, Mr. Speaker, as I did a moment ago on another subject, to do it either now or at any other time .during the present session.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I now, Mr. Speaker, invite you to listen as you have, Sir, with great attention, to this latter clause.
The Liberal Party hereby pledges itself-
Commits itself, pledges itself by its signs and seals! They are pledged to implement by legislation. Now here is what my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition had to say. After stating the constitutional position in which we now are, not under some conditions that might arise, he says it will be the duty of His Excellency to call upon him (Mr. King) to form a government. Then he said to the electors of West Peterborough, a protectionist riding:
Nothing will be done in the way of altering or amending the tariff in the smallest particular.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Finish the quotation.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend from Brome by his expression questions the accuracy of the statement.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, no; I say finish the quotation.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I will finish it. Let me read the first quotation again. There is a little danger of our getting away from the position I was trying to emphasize a minute ago:
And the Liberal Party pledges itself-
No, I am wrong it should be "hereby pledges itself." What to do? To quit and go to the country? No. "Hereby pledges itself" to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution that I have read. When? When returned to power.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When returned to
power.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Wait a moment, let me, Sir, read again what the leader of the Opposition said.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Read it in full.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the Meighen Administration is defeated "it would be the duty of His Excellency"-no option in the matter at all-"the Governor General to call upon the leader of the Opposition to form an administration." In other words he is going to accede to office by the defeat of this Government no matter how he can accomplish that defeat. My hon. friend knew when he was speaking to the electors of Peterborough that that platform would defeat him. He knew he could not carry Peterborough with that. He knows, and other hon. gentlemen that I see before me know, that they dare not go to the country on that platform. How was he to get: around that difficulty? Having shown that he was likely to get into office by defeating this Meighen Administration, which he said had not the confidence of the House - persuading them to that-how was he to still their fears about this tariff proposal to which the Liberals in a grave convention had committed themselves?
The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) in the same strain said:
Do not worry about the tariff. Remember that in 1896 and 1911 we broke all our past pledges and kept the National Policy In force.
And the hon. the leader of the Opposition said:
You are perfectly safe; nothing will be done in the way of altering or amending the tariff in the smallest particular.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He said that nothing would be done before a general election. Finish the quotation; be fair.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) has not seen the point yet. I do not like to so characterize him, Mr. Speaker, but I am forced to by his frequent interruptions-my hon. friend's mind is so constituted that he cannot keep in it two propositions at the same time.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is very smart.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We can easily understand, Mr. Speaker, how at Peterborough the hon. leader of the Opposition said he would take one course, and in his speech at Kamloops-which I am about to read to the House-he said he would take another course.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Finish the first quotation; be fair.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it will become any hon. member to reiterate at the peril of tiring the House for the benefit of one hon. gentleman who does not understand the point. My hon. friend does not want me to read this platform again, does he?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, I do.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Well, I am not going to do so. We have got that platform, Mr. Speaker, and every hon. member, except my hon. friend from Lunenburg, knows to what I refer. That platform contains this paragraph:
And the Liberal party hereby pledges itself to implement by legislation the provisions of this resolution when returned to power.
. Mr. DUFF: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Now, the hon. the leader of the Opposition told the people in Peterborough in the same speech and in almost the same paragraph that the Meighen Administration would be defeated, and that His Excellency the Governor General would then call upon him to form an administration. Having got his hearers into a state of mind where presumably they accepted that probability, he proceeded:
Nothing will be done In the way of altering or amending the tariff in the smallest particular. .
Now, my point is this-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go on.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My point is quite clear, Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Are you afraid of it?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My point is very clear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is so clear-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order. Hon. members will please bear in mind that the hon. member for Centre Vancouver has the floor.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My point is so clear, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. gentleman does not like the explanation nor the revelation of it. But in case it should be considered that I am making a play on words in connection with the various utterances of the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, let me read a portion from a verbatim

report of a speech made by him in the city of Kamloops in company with my hon. friend from Lunenburg. If he was not present that night I think he was ill.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I was on the platform.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Then the hon. member will remember and be able to verify what I am about to say. In this speech the hon. the leader of the Opposition, speaking of the general policy of the Liberal party, went on to say that they wanted a party that represented all political opinions, and classes, and so forth, and then he described how in this great convention in Ottawa there were extremists, that there were free traders and high and low protectionists-the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), for example

and that there was a great body in between, neither high protectionists nor low, nor free traders, but he said they all got together and were able to form a platform in the interests of all the people. Then he proceeded in this strain:
We say the time has come in Canada when the tariff should! be reduced.
That is a straight statement.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Very good. Then take
the following:
We will start on it at once.
When is that? Is that after a general election? My hon. friends cannot escape this, because it is too serious a matter to play ducks and drakes with, and again, I invite them to consider these statements. The hon. the leader of the Opposition stated clearly the constitutional practice, that if this resolution or amendment of his carried he would go into office, and he told the people of Kamloops that it was the intention of his party to start on the revision of the tariff at once.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
At Kamloops he said he
was going to reduce the tariff.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon.
friend has at last shown to this House that either he is not sincere or not sensible in the remarks that he has made.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I must ask the hon. gentleman to withdraw that remark.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend asks
me to withdraw my remark where I referred to him as being not sensible. Well, perhaps, Mr. Speaker, he is sensible of what I am saying, but he refuses to admit

it. I do not know which is worse-to lie ignorant of a thing', or to refuse to admit when he does understand it. The point I am seeking, and it is certainly as clear as type can make it, is that the hon. the leader of the Opposition-whom I am glad to see in his seat at the present moment, he having just arrived-makes a declaration before a protectionist constituency assuring the people that the protective principles of the tariff were perfectly safe, and that the hye-election had no bearing upon the tariff whatever; but in the West, in Kamloops, he makes the statement:
Let me tell you what that policy is. We say the time has come in Canada when the tariff should be reduced. We will start on it at once.
Then I draw the attention of the House to this as well, that in the city of Peterborough the hon. the leader of the Opposition, and also his first lieutenant the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, assured that manufacturing centre that there was no danger of tariff revision, the latter using these words:
Be not worried about the tariff. You can rest assured that there will be nothing done to disturb it.
Let me point out, Sir, that they were addressing the people of a city where they manufacture mining, flour milling, saw mill, electrical and other machinery. Listen to this. In the city of Kamloops the hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition, knowing there were men in his audience who were interested in mining, saw mill and other industries, held out this bait. I quote his exact words which were taken down verbatim:
As to the reduction of duties on the necessaries of life-food, clothing, shelter, warmth, this can be done.
Then he goes on:
It seems to me that you here in British Columbia need a reduction of the duties on the instruments of production more than any other part of the country.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that in Peterborough they manufacture machinery, and there the people were assured there would be nothing done in the way of tariff reduction. At Kamloops, where they use this machinery and where they are handicapped by the long freight haul that I referred to a moment ago, which is one of our problems, and where a great deal of similar machinery is purchased in the United States>
the hon. the leader of the Opposition told the people:
You have your forests, you have your fisheries, you have your mines. You need machinery to develop them, and if this machinery can be procured at a lower cost, it will be followed by a lower cost of production.
Then he continues:
You need a reduction of duties on the instruments of production.	[DOT]
Now, what I am driving at in my argument is simply this, that my hon. friend who leads the Opposition-and in his absence I challenged his followers, and I challenge him now that he is in his seat- dare not bring forward the Liberal platform of 1919 as an issue in this House or in the country. He went through British Columbia appealing to the people-to the selfish instincts of the people, if I may say so-with regard to certain things that they used. He went to the Prairie Provinces and met my friends opposite of the Agrarian party and told them that there was no difference between his policy and theirs; then he came down to Peterborough, a manufacturing town, and told the people that there was no danger; that the tariff would not be tampered with-that the byelection then impending would not result in any interference with the tariff.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. gentleman left out the words "until after an election."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff) is still worrying.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not nearly as much as the hon. members from Vancouver Centre.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to direct the attention of the House very briefly to another point. My hon. friends state that we have no right to bring the tariff into this discussion; that it is not of interest at the present time. I submit to you, Sir, that the matter is of vital interest. In the speech from the Throne His Excellency, on the advice of the Government, makes a clear statement of the position of the Government on the tariff. Now, I have here two motions, one moved on June 9, 1919, by the hon. member for Brome and the other on May 18, 1920, by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. I shall not weary the House by reading the resolutions, but I wish to point out that in 1919, two years ago, the member for Brome had been alot-ted the high position of financial critic of the Opposition. But he held that position only for a very short time; in fact, after he introduced this resolution he was relegated to the back benches, I might say, and replaced by another gentleman who .had less

dangerous views on the tariff. In the 1919 resolution a substantial reduction was asked for, "as speedily as may be expedient," and so on; then the member for Brome added this:
Also, the reciprocal offer of trade with the United States should be accepted.
If my hon. friends opposite are in earnest about their tariff position, all they have to do is to make a motion in the House setting forth exactly where they stand. Almost every public utterance of the leader of the Opposition has been a different utterance on the tariff question. If my hon. friends do not desire to stand by the platform of 1919, which has been sent all over this country as their official declaration; if they do not wish to stand by the resolution of the hon. member for Brome or that of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's to which I have referred, let them frame some platform or some resolution which they are prepared to stand by and introduce it into this House, and we shall be prepared to meet them.
Hon. members on this side will welcome a campaign in this country on the fiscal policy. The leader of the Opposition is seeking to hold the manufacturing interests of Eastern Canada behind him and at the same time to bewitch my hon. friends from the Prairie Provinces as well into supporting him. Why should that be? There is much more in it, perhaps, than would appear on the surface. One would think that the hon. member for Prince, the leader of the Opposition, would not take that somewhat questionable position unless there was really sound reason for his doing so. I shall now give to you, Sir, and to the House what I consider to be the exact reasons for that position. I do not expect my hon. friends immediately opposite to agree with me. but I invite the attention of every thinking member of this House to the argument that I shall make.
It is this: assuming that an election should be brought about, it is absolutely certain that the party whose destinies are now in the hands of the hon. member for Prince could not come into power. That is certain, for the simple reason that there is , not a single Liberal in the Prairie Provinces; we have the Agrarian party replacing the Liberal party in that part of the country. If this Government, or the party represented by this side of the House, should not have a majority, the only possible solution would be the formation of a coalition by hon. gentlemen immediately op-

posite and the Agrarian party. That is the only possible hope for the accession to power of hon. gentlemen immediately opposite. The leader of the Opposition knows that; therefore, he is seeking to hold the allegiance of my hon. friends from the Prairie Provinces with a view to their supporting him in case such an emergency should arise.
Let me briefly, Mr. Speaker, sum up the points I wish to make. As the leader of the Opposition is in his seat, I invite him to consider the challenge that I threw out earlier in my remarks. If the statements of njy hon. friend are true; if the "will of the people has been ignored"-I am quoting his own words; if the "rights of the people have been usurped" by this Parliament; if "hundreds of thousands of citizens were deprived of the franchise;" if the franchise of 1917 was the "worst betrayal of the rights of the people this country has ever known;" if "persons are taxed without representation;" if we are witnessing "open defiance"-still quoting my hon. friend's own words-"of the most fundamental of all principles of government;" if "these halls of Parliament"-again quoting-"are within a charnel house of disillusionment full of intrigue and deceptions" -if, Sir, all this is true; if this Parliament is properly and correctly described by the hon. gentleman in these terms, then I say he can remedy that very quickly by resigning his seat, in company with those who sit behind him. I say to him, with the utmost conviction .of the accuracy of my statements, that this Government and hon. gentlemen on this side of the House would not dare to remain in office if any such contingency arose. The leader of the Opposition knows perfectly well that he cannot get the backing of his followers sufficiently to do that; he knows that a very large proportion of his followers would desert him if there was any possibility of the Government being defeated at this time. I cannot, Sir, come to any other conclusion than that my hon. friend lacks sincerity in moving this amendment.
