speechtext: Order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I am perfectly in order.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I repeat it, Mr. Speaker, there is every evidence in the words and actions of my hon. friend and in the resolution itself that he lacks sincerity in proposing it and that his sole object is to

secure office, thinking that, perchance, with a large number of hon. gentlemen on this side away ill, he should be able to secure the reigns of office with the assistance of my hon. friends from the prairies-whose interests, I may say, are diametrically opposed to his on this occasion.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the hon. gentleman resumes his seat, I would like to inquire whether he is authorized to state on behalf of the Government that if the Opposition members will resign, the Government will resign and go to the country?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Answer.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Am I permitted to answer?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will simply repeat what I have said-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Answer.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I will answer my hon. friends. I uttered the challenge to my hon. friends that if they felt the accuracy of the statements of their leader, then it was their duty to resign the seats so obtained; that in so far as this side of the House was concerned, I was convinced, speaking for myself-

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: -and as far as I am concerned I will act as I speak. I was convinced that hon. gentlemen on this side would not dare to continue to hold office if hon. gentlemen opposite were to act as 1 have suggested.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, my first remarks must be words of protest. I hold in my hand the invitation sent to the members of my family asking them to assist at the opening of Parliament as well as an attached memorandum. These documents are exclusively written out in English. To say the least, such a proceeding implies towards the members of this House belonging to the French race, a lack of courtesy which cannot be condoned and which for my part I strongly resent. Indeed, I hold, Mr. Speaker, that invitations of that kind should be couched in the two official languages recognized in this country and that the opposite practice cannot be tolerated. Consequently, I beg of the competent authorities to put an end to that wretched practice, tending to set aside the rights of the French langurge, in such matters.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
During the month of
September 1920, I had some business to transact, on behalf of a French-Canadian, with the officials of the Canadian National Railways system. The negotiations involved the signing of a deed. We had requested that the deed should be written in French. But here is the answer that we received:
jLfivis, 2i8th September, 19'20.
Mr. Arthur Trahan, M.P.,
Nicolet.
Dear Sir,
In answer to yours of the 18th instant, I hereby send you a form of application re the laying through of telephone wires over our property at Lemieux.
I am sorry that I am unable to send you a form in French, but we have none printed in this language at this time.
And the form in question, Mr. Speaker, contains two printed pages bearing especially on the construction of sidings. We are always met by the same old excuse which indicates, as far as the Government . and its officials are concerned, that they are intent on making difficulties when it is a question of respecting the rights of the French language in this country. I wish to say that we have refused to sign that deed written in English and we do not intend doing so as long as they will not supply us with a French form. These few cases, chosen among thousands of others, show clearly to what extent the rights of the French language are disregarded in governmental spheres. I most strongly protest against that scandalous policy, and I wish to proclaim before all, that Canada is a bilingual country and both official languages, in practice, and the constitution as well, must be respected. When I demand from the Government that they do not illegally restrict the use of the French language, not only I exercise a right which is inscribed in the constitution but I fulfil a sacred duty.
Indeed, there is something more, something better than the commercial and industrial wealth of a race: it is the thought and the language which expresses it. It is through the diffusion of its language that a nation shows its external vitality, it is through the radiation of its ideals that it preserves and expands its influence. Mr. Speaker, we all wish to see Canada a united country. Let us see that French and English have an equal share in this magni-ficient Parliament, let us treat both languages with the same respect and deference.
I

It is generally admitted to-day that a knowledge of French is necessary not only in this country but also with reference to foreign intercourse; even the hon. member for Durham (Hon Mr. Rowell) who is not friendly to our language, lately proclaimed the necessity of a bilingual education.
People praise the beauty of our mother tongue, and rightly so. May I quote on the subject a few beautiful thoughts uttered by Mr. Etienne Lamy at the sitting of the French Academy held on the 20th of December, 1917:
"When Cardinal de Richelieu founded our Academy, he had these words engraved upon the seal: To immortality. It was to the French language that Richelieu wished that future. It inherited that power of universality which the Greek and afterwards the Latin languages had obtained. But nowadays this supremacy of yore needs being upheld. Outside, it still commands the admiration of the high cultured, though these at times, are repelled by the works of some of our writers. We must admit that those delinquencies are diseases of but a few and of short duration ; that the clearness, order, grace and harmony of the French language are the elements of .its primitive, unalterable 'and unequalled character; that these attainments find their usefulness beyond its native land ; that it is not only an idiom for the use of a particular people, but an instrument of preciseness at the service of the human mind and the purest crystal through which light filters without deviating."
I wish that every one of my colleagues would meditate over these great truths and they will understand why I protest against those who ignore the rights of the French language and that I intend to uphold, to safeguard and to spread it through Canada.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
(Translation) The Government is not merely satisfied with putting obstacles in our way concerning the use of the Franch language; but it really seems firmly resolved to encroach as often as possible upon the legitimate right of the Catholic people to adhere to the practice of their religion. Probably for the first time since Confederation the Catholic public employees have been compelled to work on holy days, observed by them like' Sundays, and this occurred not only in Ottawa, but also in the city of Quebec.
Yet, last session when we opposed the Senate's amendment to do away with several legal holidays, which coincided with Catholic holy days, the then Prime Minister the hon. member from King's, Nova Scotia (Sir Robert Borden), stated that the Catholic employees had no reason whatever to be alarmed, since leave of absence would be granted to them on those days. Notwith-
[Mr Trahan.]
standing that specific pledge, an official notice from the Postmaster General's Department, presided' over by the amazing Mr. Blondin, ordered that the post office employees of the city of Quebec should work on All Saints' Day as on all other days; and if I am correctly informed, Catholic public servants in Ottawa were placed under the same obligation. The same thing occurred here on Conception Day and on Epiphany Day.
Why has not the present Prime Minister kept the pledge given by his predecessor and why has he permitted such spiteful measures to be enacted against the Catholics of this country? I hold him responsible for this outrage against our Catholic convictions and for this attack against our dignity and our religious liberty. We hope that such a thing will not occur again and we hope the Government will take such steps that Catholic holy days will be recognized both by this Government and this Parliament.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
When the Government, as I have just mentioned fails to keep the promises made before this House, it is no longer worthy of the confidence of the people. Therefore, the leader of the Opposition is justified in moving his amendment and we, the representatives of the province of Quebec, have ample grounds to question tne good faith of the Prime Minister who professes friendship for us. His deeds are fewer than his words and these vary according to his audience whether he addresses a French or an English audience.
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister came to the Province of Quebec during the course of last summer; he spoke both at Sherbrooke and at Granby; there he told us that he always had a tender spot for the Province of Quebec, that never had he wished to do it the least injustice, nor had a thought of insinuation against the character of its people ever entered his head. It is well; we take note of it. However, later on, a partial election took place in British Columbia, which brought to this House the hon. member (Mr. MacKelvie) who seconded the address and who is deserving of our congratulations on the manner with which he has performed his delicate task. The Prime Minister took part in this contest of Yale-Cariboo, went around the country and more particularly spoke in such places as Penticton and Summerland. What; views did he express at those meetings? I have

before me the account given to a number of newspapers by the associated press. The Vancouver Sun of November the 4th, 1920, tells us that the Prime Minister discussed before the electors of Penticton and Sum-merland the question of conscription and the Military Service Act, and took advantage of this occasion to accuse the Leader of the Opposition of having left this country at a critical moment to obtain a large prebend in a foreign country and in the employ of the world's most powerful organization. The Prime Minister knew that he was far from the truth when he brought forward this accusation, knowing fully well that at the last session, the Leader of the Opposition had explained his position clearly and explicitly, which allowed of no contradiction. Following up this attack he turned against the Leader of the Opposition's supporters whom you all know; three quarters hail from the Province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, let us not forget that in this modern world, military imperialism is but the mail fist of commerce and industry *- the open field which remains to imperialism is its economical conquest of the world. These are the underlying reasons why industrial expansion is pressed to its utmost. The Government, faithful servant to the powerful financial interests, has been induced into this prodigious error: they wish to establish an "industrial Holy Empire" in Canada. While they give supremacy to industrial and military matters, they neglect the agricultural interests. Yet rural population is dwindling, the cities are overcrowded, the cost of living is high and the world is starving.
Is excessive industrialism a remedy for these evils? I will answer-No. I certainly do not wish to replace the factory by the farm nor the labourer by the farmer, but I maintain that a just equilibrium must be upheld between the agricultural and industrial interests. On the other hand I assert together with the best known economists that nothing durable, economically, socially and morally, can be built that has not agriculture as its base.
Furthermore, it is my humble opinion, that the systematic industrialization of Canada would entail the complete upheaval of this country's organization, a radical change in all our customs as well as in our ways of thinking; the future of Canada would thus be imperilled. It is pertinent to the general interest, to remain faithful to our traditions and uphold our natural inclination for agriculture. An immense territory capable of sustaining a population of tens
of millions is ours; yet we are obliged to import agricultural products. Is this not a national calamity? In a great measure, is the reason not to be found in the Government's bad policy? This Government which today presides over the destinies of our country instead of creating amongst the people a love for agriculture, has tried to inculcate in these populations the germ of militarism. That is why instead of having experimental farms in large numbers, they established here and there over the whole country, one for each county, if I am not mistaken, military halls and armouries. I maintain that it is more important to change the trend of thought of our people than to increase our armaments. We have to resist plutocratic barbarity represented by the powerful financial concerns who wish to place before all their commercial and industrial interests, that is to say economical imperialism:	we have to
struggle against social barbarity represented by these bolshevick tendencies who aim at destroying the foundation of property owhership in our country; lastly we have to fight against this barbarity under the disguise of science and learning that wish by all means possible to do away with religious teachings in our schools. What are the means at our disposal to enable us to destroy these three plagues, if it is not to turn to our most steadfast population, that one which is most attached to its native soil, the most patriotic, that is the agricultural population, is it not also to encourage farming and return to mother earth.
Such is the right principle; oppose agricultural and economic nationalism to economic imperialism, and that is the reason why the Liberal party, in framing its programme, included the interests of the farming class, and advocated the proper means to improve their condition.
Sir, "the crisis of all crises is that of moral sense", said a French writer. The Government have done nothing to check it. On the contrary, they countenance it. That was lately demonstrated to us in a pitiful manner. We had a further proof of it when in the soldiers' pensions' Act they caused to be inserted a section by which for the first time in the history of Canada our legislators granted a premium to concubinage and adultery. When it was moved that a pension be given to the "unmarried wives and mothers" according to the expression coined by Mr. Nickle, the then representative for Kingston, we of the Liberal party protested against such a disgrace; not only



we protested, but we voted against such a motion.
My right hon. friend said that we were among those who would have others fight for them and that such is our conception of liberty. For the enlightenment of my English-speaking friends, I shall quote from the Gazette:
"Again at Summerland he referred to the leader and opponents of the Government as those "whose idea of liberty was to let other people fight for them."
I need not repeat it, Sir, the large majority, 75 per cent of the followers of the leader of the Opposition came from the province of Quebec, and it is the Prime Minister himself who goes into an English speaking province and states that the followers of the leader of the Opposition are people who would have others fight for them, that is, people who are not brave enough to defend their liberty. That is tantamount to repeating in a different form the charges uttered against the province of Quebec, to wit, that the inhabitants of that province were cowards and defaulters. Our Prime Minister is still what he was in 1917, that is a downright imperialist always fighting vigourously those who do not sanction his policy of sacrificing our last man and our last dollar for the benefit of the Empire to the detriment of Canada. ,
Having discussed for some time with the hon. Minister of Marine (Mr. C. C. Ballan-tyne) the setting forward of the hands of the clock in Quebec, the hon. member from St. Hyancinthe came to an understanding, so he says, with the Postmaster touching the questions of imperialism and protection. Well, so much the worse for the hon. member if he wishes to disown his past "to curse the spirit of his race" and to set up treason as a state of policy.
As for us, we shall forever assert as in the past that above financial and monetary matters, there is our honesty of conscience to be consulted and our national pride to be safeguarded. We shall show a persistent tenacity and united stubborness in demanding an apology from those who have abused and despised us in 1917 and who now deluge us with hypocritical compliments and adulations with the sole end of dividing us upon an economic question. We shall safely keep stored in our minds, the bottom of our hearts, the rememberance of the momentous days of 1917-1918 when, under the leadership of the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we felt that we were banded together by our common trials and

our anxiety for the public safety. We shall not graciously lower our prestige by joining the ranks of the moneyed interests but true to our motto, we shall still* form an invincible alliance of true hearts, of upright thoughts and strong will power so as to maintain in their entirety our religious ideal and the purest of our national traditions.
We cannot trust those who, by the unfair war time elections Act have usurped power in 1917 and secured their ends by stirring hatred, awakening distrust and using false pretences. They have soand-olously deceived the farmers of this country when after the election they set aside the exemptions .they had solemnly promised to their sons by an Order in Council passed before the election. They deceived our clergy concerning the exemptions to clergymen and to-day they give us but the shadow of a responsible government. How? First of all, the government declines to hand over to the representatives of the people documents and information concerning the other nations.
When, in several instances, we asked for copies of the correspondence concerning the establishment of an embassy in Washington, he refused to bring down these papers, thus trampling upon the puroga-iives of Parliament-Moreover, at the time of the debate on the Peace Treaty, during the second session of 1919, he ignomin-ously treated the members of this House and the people of this country. When I asked if our delegates to the conference had or had not opposed clause 10 of the covenant, it was not thought proper to answer and frankly admit the truth, the whole truth of the matter. Is this not, Mr. Speaker, a contempt of the rights of the people, this systematically hiding the truth from its representatives? We were treated in this unceremonious way because at that time, the treaty had to be ratified without reserve and above all without delay-England, it appears, wanted it so- whatever be the consequences for Canada, and the Government, slaves to Downing street, disregarded their partisans, parliamentary institutions and the popular rights, by rushing the hasty and ill considered ratification of a treaty in connection with which they now ask for the repeal of one most important clause.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, the Government involves the country's credit and sets up new administrative machinery without the consent of Parliament. I do not need to refer again to the instance

mentioned by the hon. member for Benuce (Mr. Belaud) in the matter of the purchasing commission. The project of such a commission had been kbenly opposed on the floor of this House by the members of both sides of the House, and the Borden government had thought best not to insist upon the adoption of such a project. But the hon.
. Prime Minister had no sooner taken hold of the reins of power than, without consulting Parliament, notwithstanding the clearly expressed will of the representatives of the people on both sides of the House, he created by a simple Order in Council, this purchasing commission which no one had consented to.
MEMBERS: Shame, shame!

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And
there is another matter to which I wish to draw the attention of the House:	The
Government involves the credit of the country without consulting Parliament.
_ One day the hon. Minister of Marine got it into his head that a navy was necessary for Canada, and thereupon he entered into negotiations with the Imperial authorities to obtain warships. We have asked for the correspondence on the subject. The hon. Minister of Marine never brought it down; and it is only when he needed money for the upkeep and' equipment of these warships that he put the matter before Parliament. Is this the act of a responsible government? I respectfully claim that it is not. And in regard to this question of a navy, I mean to repeat what I said last year, that the time is exceedingly ill chosen in which to launch such a project, owing to the lamentable situation of our finances, the country being on the verge of bankruptcy. There are numberless reasons for which we should oppose this project, and I ask, why create a navy at the present hour ? Is not the League of Nations a safeguard against the recurrence of wars? Is not the limitation of armaments throughout the world the main object of the league? Large amounts are expended by us to send delegates to the meetings of the League of Nations, and with what result? What country is expected to wage war on us? I shall here take the liberty of quoting from an article of the Farmers Sun dated December 31, 1920:
"What, then are we to prepare for? To take part in another European war for which the seeds have already been sown. If the nations of Europe cannot after the awful experiences flat have occured since 1914, agree to live in peace with each other, then let European nations themselves pay the penalty. In fighting
1B|
one war to end war Canada has done her share and more than her share in that sort of experiment to ensure world peace."
These sentiments I agree with, and I claim that the time is ill chosen for the establishment of a navy in this country, especially when in all the countries of the world is mooted the question of disarmament.
The newspapers tell us that an Imperial Conference is to take place in June next, and that the Prime Ministers of the different Dominions are to be requested to take part in that conference-evidently the questions to be taken up at that conference will be of capital importance, not only for the Empire, but also for Canada.
These questions may be of two kinds: Those bearing upon our constitutional relations with the Empire, with England, and others relating to the scheme for Imperial defence announced by the Prime Minister of Great Britain in an interview in which he declared that Great Britain cannot afford to meet alone the cost of Imperial defence, and that the different dominions and colonies must contribute their share of the expense. If it is a matter of determining the constitutional relations of Canada with England, I mean to reiterate the policy adopted by the Liberal party at the national conference of August, 1919, when they opposed all centralized Imperial control, and claimed that no change in our constitutional relations with Great Britain should come into force before having been submitted to the approbation of the Canadian Parliament and ratified by the people by means of a referendum.
I share entirely, on this point, the opinion expressed by a newspaper of Toronto, the World, which is edited, if I am not mistaken, by one of the hon. members of this House (Mr. W. F. McLean) :
Canada must remain master of its own destinies, free to govern itself and to do her own wishes. The Canadian people will not tolerate to be led nor domineered by Downing Street.
We intend to preserve the supremacy we have acquired and we shall not permit any council or conference, or the imperial parliament, or any outside tribunal, to dictate to Canada. Our legislators must be of our own choice. They must not transfer their power to arty one not designated by the people. They are not the masters but the servants of the State. This authority conferred upon them cannot be transferred to other delegates such as to any imperial government. Let the Knights of the Round Table understand once for all that the Prime Minister Meighen or any other prime minister cannot alter by an iota the absolute right the people of Canada possess to govern this country. This country belongs to Canadians and they intend-to govern it as they please.

"When we shall need an advice from the Lords or their equals living outside of Canada, we shall ask for it. If in the past the Government of the Dominion has pledged Its word in any way, let it render an account to Parliament and the people.
As to the question of Imperial defence, I ask: Why this military imperialism at a time when general disarmament is the main talk everywhere?
To-day much is said about divorce in our country. The newspapers are discussing the question, and there is talk of legalizing in Canada this social cancer which is eating the heart of other countries. According to the unanimous opinion of the most distinguished jurists, the indissolubility of marriage is the rule, at least as regards the provinces of Quebec and Ontario. Those who obtain a divorce by means of a Private Bill have their marriage dissolved, but that does not change the general rule, which is the indissolubility of marriage. This principle conforms with the natural law, while the divorce, which dissolves marriage during the lifetime of the united parties is contrary to natural order.
I am not discussing this question from a religious point of view, I only look at it from a social and a national standpoint; and as such I may quote a few thoughts from a writer, which I submit to the serious consideration of the hon. members of this House:
"The indissolubility of marriage is not a religious superstition, an invention of adherents to a by-gone cult, an unreasonable enactment of wild troglodytes. Nature is at the bottom of this iron law."
And further on the author shows that divorce is not only against nature but antinational and immoral:
"Divorce, encouraged, vulgarized by a regime which confounds cowardly sentimentality with courageous and sane humaneness, divorce at will is the greatest of our crimes and the most baneful of our errors.
If we do not apply the hot iron to this ulcer, our blood will continue to ooze from it in corruption.
But, it will be said, what of the rights of man and the rights of woman... the right to live...
What! what rights?... Tou have children, you belong to them! you made a mistake, so much the worse! Tou are already of the past. The child is the future, he is the race. Remain bound together by the child."
And farther on-*
"It takes twenty years to make a human being capable of facing life. It is not the work of a day dr of a month, it is a considerable labour which is the whole raison d'etre of parents and shows the importance which Nature attaches to manhood and what responsibilities it entails. Tou aim at shunning these responsibilities, eschewing the family and its duties by the selfishness of celibacy or the shame of

divorce. Flee! but in your flight you drag all - with you to the abyss, and the country perishes through your desertion of the hearth."

speechtext:
Henri de Noussanne. A little farther on he says:
"Marriage is worth what we are "worth. From money calculations, vanities, lies, IIewdress, . can happiness be expected? The intoxication of pride once over, The veil once fallen from folly, one finds oneself in a hell. One then believes that the way out of it is divorce, and in this plight, pledges and children are forgotten. The coward and perjurer, imagines that it matters not; there will be no consequences, no morrow. Marriage is thought to be a transitory, an occasional adventure, dependent only upon one's calculations, one's mood.
".A.S well believe that birth and death are also dependent upon our whim, and renewable at our caprice. As well imagine that we can fool Nature, as we can fool men, and that God is not the name of the Spirit in Nature, and that justice is not the name of reason in the spirit."
And in another place the author again
says:
"We can only expect our salvation from social peace made of family peace, which can only come from the purification and the consolidation of marriage restored by its essential function, which is the creation and education of the child."
Well, Mr. Speaker, we complain at present of unrest, in certain parts of Canada. This unrest can be attributed to the dire ravages caused by divorce and the reduction of the birth-rate. We hope that the Government will not propose so iniquitous a measure as one for the establishment of a divorce court. We hope that directly or indirectly they will hot favour such a measure, and I for one, should it be brought, will hold it my duty to most vigorously oppose it.
Nowadays compliments are freely lavished upon the province of Quebec. It is called the pivot of Confederation. We hear that her people are sane, are stable and do not allow themselves to he blinded by socialistic or other passions; and it is true. Why is this the case in our province? It is because we have remained attached to the native soil, to peaceful country life, we have sought before all to develop our agricultural lands, to throw them open to colonization. Why have the people of Quebec acquired such a good reputation in the other provinces? Because in the humble school in which they are formed they are taught their duties towards God and towards their neighbours. On this point let me quote from a speech delivered by the new Prime Minister (Hon. Mr. Taschereau), on November 4th, 1920, on the occasion of the

meeting of the deputy-ministers of education of the different provinces.
However behind the times, did he say, our primary schools may have seemed to you some twenty-five yeans ago, I can say this much to their credit. They taught the children their religious duties, and they taught them to remain on the land with their parents; they warded off that modern evil which draws the farmers' sons from their natural sphere; they , did not seek to lead them towards a commercial or industrial life which has no right to claim them, nor to take them away from the pursuit of agriculture.
I have said enough and perhaps too much, Mr. Speaker, to show that the Government is undeserving of the confidence of this House and of the country, as the amendment of the hon. leader of the Opposition shows. The Government ignores, notwithstanding our constitution, the rights of the French language; they do violence to our Catholic conscience in forcing the civil employees to work on religious holidays; they continue their tactic of insulting the province of Quebec while seeming to court it; they give us a caricature of responsible government by refusing to furnish the people/s representatives with the public documents to which they are entitled; they pledge the credit of the country without consulting Parliament; they work for the triumph of economic and military imperialism to the detriment of agricultural and economic nationalism; they, in a word, tend, by means of divers laws which they have passed and others of which they underhandedly favour the adoption, they tend, I say, towards the crisis of all crises, that of moral sense. We oppose such a policy. We of the province of Quebec wish to live in the tranquility of work and order, by which may be insured the harmonious development of our country under the moral aegis of a religion which connects Heaven overhead with Mother Earth.
On the motion of Mr. C. R. Harrison (Nipissing) the debate was adjourned.
On the motion of Hon. Mr. Ballantyne, the House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
Wednesday, February 23, 1921.
